Who introduced the terms neonatology and neonatologist in the cited historical account?
column2:
Alexander Schaffer. Schaffer introduced these terms in the preface to Diseases of the Newborn in 1960.

PDF p. 21

column1: Which early research themes were associated with Barcroft and Dawes?
column2:
Barcroft and Dawes: fetal gas exchange. Barcroft and Dawes investigated placental transfer and fetal oxygen physiology, illustrating the basic-science roots of care.

PDF p. 21

column1: What did the ACTH experience teach about interpreting a dramatic individual response?
column2:
No greater efficacy than placebo, with adverse effects. The initial response did not predict trial benefit. The placebo-controlled study found no greater efficacy and identified steroid adverse effects.

PDF p. 32

column1: What role did the Cochrane Collaboration take in neonatal evidence development?
column2:
Systematic reviews from the Cochrane Collaboration. The chapter describes the 1993 Cochrane Collaboration as producing and disseminating systematic reviews of therapies.

PDF p. 32

column1: What historical incubator practice contributed to retinopathy of prematurity?
column2:
Retinopathy associated with excessive oxygen exposure. The chapter links high inspired oxygen concentrations in leakproof incubators to the epidemic of retrolental fibroplasia/retinopathy.

PDF p. 28

column1: What two broad domains should accompany evaluation of a new neonatal technology?
column2:
Assess intended benefit and unintended harm, including later outcomes; a promising individual response is not sufficient evidence of treatment efficacy.

PDF p. 32

column1: Why should relative risk be accompanied by absolute risk?
column2:
Relative effects match, but absolute differences differ. The absolute increases are 0.1 and 10 percentage points. Equal relative effects need not have equal clinical impact.

PDF p. 39

column1: Why is single-factor causality difficult to infer for common prematurity morbidities?
column2:
Multiple component causes and their sequence may contribute. The text describes IVH, NEC and BPD as multifactorial, with causes that can be unknown, unmeasured or time dependent.

PDF p. 39

column1: What is the purpose of epidemiology in neonatal-perinatal medicine?
column2:
Epidemiology. Epidemiology studies population health and disease, risk factors and associations, including mortality as an indicator of health and care.

PDF p. 39

column1: Which signs are included in the cited definition of live birth?
column2:
A definite sign of life such as heartbeat. Breathing or another definite sign of life after delivery qualifies; cord cutting and placental separation are not prerequisites.

PDF p. 40

column1: What can maternal and infant mortality indicators help assess?
column2:
Assess population health, access and quality in context. Mortality rates inform assessment of population health and care systems, but interpretation requires context and consistent definitions.

PDF p. 39

column1: What is the risk difference when risk rises from 10% to 20%?
column2:
10 percentage points, or 0.10 as a proportion. The relative risk is 2; these are different measures of effect.

PDF p. 39

column1: How do structured and unstructured neonatal data differ?
column2:
Coded gestational age: structured; free-text note: unstructured. Structured data use predefined fields or coding; free text, pictures and audio are examples of unstructured information.

PDF p. 47

column1: What must happen before a large neonatal dataset can reliably inform care?
column2:
Curate, organize, explore and validate the data. The chapter emphasizes preparation, accessibility and validation; a large volume alone does not establish usefulness.

PDF p. 47

column1: What is ascertainment bias in neonatal database research?
column2:
Ascertainment bias from changed identification. The chapter uses this example to show how changing recognition and classification can produce an apparent incidence increase.

PDF p. 50

column1: When can neonatal database studies be particularly useful?
column2:
Generate and investigate hypotheses while addressing bias. Large observational datasets can investigate questions difficult to randomize, but their design and bias limitations remain.

PDF p. 49

column1: How can neonatal databases support quality improvement?
column2:
Consistent process and outcome definitions. Pre-existing, consistent measures allow services to track change and collaborate on quality improvement.

PDF p. 50

column1: Does a large database replace a prospective randomized trial?
column2:
No. It can reveal associations, rare events and care patterns and generate hypotheses, but confounding, classification and other biases remain important.

PDF p. 47

column1: What does medical ethics involve in neonatal care?
column2:
Reasoned evaluation of benefits, burdens and values. Ethical reasoning evaluates and justifies action in pursuit of well-being, while recognizing uncertainty and differing values.

PDF p. 58

column1: What is the central balance in neonatal shared decision making?
column2:
Partnership balancing parental authority and professional beneficence. The chapter describes a partnership through mutual consent, balancing parental authority with obligations to the infant.

PDF p. 62

column1: Why may an information-only decision model be insufficient for parents?
column2:
Emotions and lived experience can shape how information is used. Parents may use affective and experience-based reasoning; understanding facts alone does not complete supportive communication.

PDF p. 62

column1: How can physiologic and quality-of-life definitions of viability differ?
column2:
Physiologic possibility versus an explicit value judgment. The chapter separates physiologic maintenance of life from quality-of-life considerations that incorporate judgments about morbidity.

PDF p. 66

column1: What relationship underpins neonatal ethical practice in the chapter?
column2:
A patient-parent-clinician relationship built on trust and the infant’s good. The chapter describes a relationship of mutual trust, clinical competence and moral discretion directed toward the newborn and family.

PDF p. 58

column1: Why should ethical counseling make professional reasoning transparent?
column2:
Transparency helps parents understand the clinical considerations and values informing a recommendation and supports deliberation within a partnership.

PDF p. 62

column1: How does the Donabedian framework organize quality measures?
column2:
Structure, process and outcome. Structure concerns the care setting, process concerns care activities, and outcomes are their results.

PDF p. 90

column1: What are the core elements of the Model for Improvement?
column2:
Measurable aim, tracked measures, changes and PDSA cycles. The model combines specific aims, measures over time, strategic change ideas and iterative PDSA learning.

PDF p. 90

column1: Why are balancing measures needed?
column2:
Track growth as a balancing measure alongside the target. Balancing measures detect related outcomes that may worsen while the target improves; the chapter gives this feeding-growth example.

PDF p. 94

column1: How should shared care baselines handle individual patient needs?
column2:
Adapt care, document the deviation and learn from it. Shared baselines reduce unwarranted variation while allowing justified individualization and subsequent refinement.

PDF p. 91

column1: Why do stable agreed definitions matter in neonatal quality measurement?
column2:
Reconcile definitions and assess comparability. Clear, stable definitions across time and location are essential for interpreting differences and comparing NICUs.

PDF p. 92

column1: What should a NICU quality review include besides quantitative outcome data?
column2:
Input from staff and families and examination of the local context and care processes; these inform where and how improvement is attempted.

PDF p. 84

column1: What is the patient-safety rationale for simulation?
column2:
Repeated practice in a safe simulated setting. Simulation permits repeated practice and remediation before patient exposure, consistent with avoiding preventable harm.

PDF p. 119

column1: Why does a fixed training duration not establish competence?
column2:
Judge demonstrated performance rather than attendance alone. Learners have different experience, strengths and learning rates; time spent does not by itself show successful performance.

PDF p. 119

column1: How does debriefing differ from briefing and one-way feedback?
column2:
Debriefing. Debriefing discusses completed events through interaction; briefing concerns planned events, and feedback can flow one way.

PDF p. 122

column1: What additional safety benefit can in situ simulation provide?
column2:
Identification of a latent safety threat. In situ simulation can uncover equipment, personnel and communication problems in the actual clinical environment.

PDF p. 123

column1: What does Helping Babies Breathe illustrate about fidelity?
column2:
Appropriate low-fidelity simulation can be effective. Helping Babies Breathe is described as a successful low-fidelity approach adapted to resource-limited settings.

PDF p. 122

column1: What should a simulation program do when weaknesses become apparent?
column2:
Identify and remediate them through suitable practice, feedback and, where appropriate, debriefing rather than treating participation alone as competence.

PDF p. 119

column1: Which broad approach supports neonatal survival in resource-limited settings?
column2:
Adaptable packages spanning maternal and essential newborn care. The chapter highlights essential newborn care, resuscitation programs and maternal-newborn packages suited to wider implementation.

PDF p. 127

column1: What core-temperature threshold defines hypothermia in this source?
column2:
Hypothermia because it is below 36.5°C. The chapter defines neonatal hypothermia below 36.5°C and notes that it can occur even in warm seasons.

PDF p. 137

column1: Which routine practices can contribute to neonatal hypothermia?
column2:
These practices can contribute to preventable heat loss. Early bathing, inadequate clothing and losses during transport are described causes of neonatal hypothermia.

PDF p. 138

column1: How can trained workers assess possible neonatal sepsis when laboratory access is limited?
column2:
Use validated clinical-sign assessment, initiate indicated care and triage. The chapter describes clinical-sign algorithms to support recognition, treatment initiation and referral where laboratory access is limited.

PDF p. 138

column1: What care domains accompany respiratory treatment for preterm infants?
column2:
Thermoregulation, nutrition and sepsis prevention/treatment. The chapter emphasizes several effective care domains; a respiratory intervention does not replace thermal, nutritional and infection care.

PDF p. 135

column1: Why should an intervention’s feasibility and coverage be considered in global newborn care?
column2:
Population benefit depends on delivering effective care at scale within the local health system, not solely on efficacy in a highly resourced unit.

PDF p. 139

column1: How do infant and neonatal mortality periods differ?
column2:
Infant: within one year; neonatal: within 28 days. The chapter distinguishes death within one year from death within the neonatal period of 28 days.

PDF p. 150

column1: What are social determinants of health?
column2:
Social determinants of health. Social determinants include conditions and wider systems shaping how people live and their access to resources and opportunities.

PDF p. 159

column1: How does the chapter frame race in interpreting health disparities?
column2:
Examine socially structured inequities rather than assuming innate racial biology. The chapter describes race as a socially defined category and emphasizes inequities affecting outcomes.

PDF p. 159

column1: When should efforts to improve maternal health and access begin?
column2:
Improve maternal health and equitable access before conception and across care. The source emphasizes maternal health before conception and accessible, affordable, equitable maternal-child care.

PDF p. 161

column1: Why may nominal availability of health services be insufficient?
column2:
Practical barriers to accessible care. The chapter identifies provider maldistribution and transport barriers in urban settings as well as limited services in remote areas.

PDF p. 161

column1: Why is improving NICU care alone unlikely to resolve population-level neonatal disparities?
column2:
Relevant influences include maternal health, poverty, access to care, insurance, education, housing and other structural conditions across the life course.

PDF p. 150

column1: What family pattern commonly characterizes autosomal recessive disease?
column2:
Horizontal transmission among siblings. Two pathogenic alleles can produce disease in siblings of unaffected heterozygous parents.

PDF p. 171

column1: What is the origin of the fetal-associated DNA signal used in maternal cfDNA screening?
column2:
Placental trophoblast. The detectable fetal-associated DNA in maternal blood is of placental origin.

PDF p. 177

column1: What tissue is sampled by chorionic villus sampling?
column2:
Placental villi. CVS obtains placental tissue, usually at 10–13 weeks, for genetic diagnosis.

PDF p. 181

column1: What major diagnostic advantage does microarray offer over routine karyotyping?
column2:
Chromosomal microarray for small copy-number changes. Microarrays detect smaller copy-number gains and losses than routine karyotypes.

PDF p. 183

column1: How should pregnancy affect decisions about necessary diagnostic imaging?
column2:
Balance exposure risk against the risk of delayed diagnosis. Appropriate test selection and modification reduce exposure, while delayed diagnosis can also harm mother and fetus.

PDF p. 174

column1: What distinction should be maintained between a screening result and a genetic diagnosis?
column2:
Screening estimates risk; diagnostic modalities examine appropriate fetal or placental samples to establish the tested genetic finding.

PDF p. 181

column1: How does ultrasound frequency affect penetration and resolution?
column2:
Lower frequency improves penetration while higher frequency improves resolution. Probe choice balances lower-frequency penetration against higher-frequency spatial resolution.

PDF p. 188

column1: Why is coupling gel applied for an ultrasound examination?
column2:
Optimize sound transmission. Water-based gel serves as a coupling agent for ultrasound transmission.

PDF p. 188

column1: Which two mechanisms underlie recognized ultrasound bioeffects?
column2:
Heating and cavitation. The source identifies heating and cavitation as mechanisms of ultrasound bioeffects.

PDF p. 190

column1: Why is obstetric ultrasound training important?
column2:
Underdiagnosis or overdiagnosis causing harmful clinical decisions. Misinterpretation can trigger harmful downstream decisions; specific training and continued competence matter.

PDF p. 191

column1: What sonographic structure confirms an intrauterine pregnancy site?
column2:
An intrauterine pregnancy site. A yolk sac or embryo within the uterus confirms that pregnancy site; it does not establish genetics or future outcome.

PDF p. 193

column1: Why should a suspected early pregnancy failure not be diagnosed from a single rigid visualization threshold?
column2:
Serum hCG and visualization thresholds vary; the source emphasizes waiting beyond usual developmental thresholds before diagnosing failure.

PDF p. 193

column1: Why must fetal surveillance results be interpreted in clinical context?
column2:
False-positive results are possible and clinical context matters. Tests reflect biophysical correlates of hypoxemia and have false-positive results; not all causes of stillbirth are predictable.

PDF p. 229

column1: What acceleration pattern defines a reactive NST in the described standard criterion?
column2:
At least two accelerations of 15 beats/min lasting at least 15 seconds. The described reactive NST has at least two accelerations peaking 15 beats/min above baseline and lasting at least 15 seconds.

PDF p. 230

column1: How are individual biophysical profile components scored?
column2:
Each component receives either 0 or 2 points. The five components are assigned 0 or 2 points, yielding an even total between 0 and 10.

PDF p. 231

column1: What AFI threshold defines oligohydramnios in this source?
column2:
Oligohydramnios. The source defines oligohydramnios by AFI of 5 cm or less, or no single vertical pocket greater than 2 cm.

PDF p. 232

column1: How can oxytocin-associated tachysystole contribute to an abnormal fetal heart pattern?
column2:
Reduce or discontinue oxytocin as clinically indicated. Resolving tachysystole can improve fetal status; excessive contraction frequency limits recovery.

PDF p. 240

column1: What should usually follow a maternal report of decreased fetal movement?
column2:
Clinical evaluation is usually appropriate; the source does not identify one optimal formal kick-count strategy or clear prevention benefit from routine quantified counting.

PDF p. 230

column1: Why is maternal risk central to fetal-surgery consent?
column2:
Maternal procedural risks and available alternatives. Anesthesia, surgery and continued pregnancy expose the mother to risks, so counseling must cover these and alternatives.

PDF p. 243

column1: What anatomy does ultrasound help define before fetal intervention?
column2:
Placental location, fetal position and maternal vessels. Ultrasound defines the lesion, placental anatomy, fetal position and maternal vessels and supports fetal monitoring.

PDF p. 243

column1: What does fetoscopy add to needle-based fetal access?
column2:
Fetoscopic access. A fetoscope permits direct visualization while ultrasound continues to support safe access.

PDF p. 244

column1: Why does open fetal hysterotomy affect future delivery planning?
column2:
Uterine rupture risk requiring cesarean delivery in future pregnancies. The source describes mandatory cesarean delivery after fetal-surgery hysterotomy because of rupture risk.

PDF p. 244

column1: What physiologic support is maintained during EXIT?
column2:
EXIT with uteroplacental circulation maintained. EXIT maintains uteroplacental circulation during the fetal intervention and is followed by delivery once the airway is established.

PDF p. 244

column1: Why is maternal hemorrhage a particular concern during EXIT?
column2:
Uterine relaxation is necessary during the intervention but increases hemorrhage risk; coordinated anesthesia and surgical management is essential.

PDF p. 244

column1: How can prior lead exposure affect a fetus during pregnancy?
column2:
Lead mobilized from maternal bone. Lead accumulates in bone and can be mobilized during pregnancy and transported to the fetus.

PDF p. 261

column1: What is paraoccupational toxicant exposure?
column2:
Paraoccupational exposure. Occupational chemicals brought home on clothes or materials can expose household members.

PDF p. 262

column1: How do most xenobiotics cross the placenta?
column2:
Passive diffusion. Most xenobiotics cross by passive diffusion, with gradients and placental flow influencing fetal exposure.

PDF p. 264

column1: Why can amniotic fluid prolong exposure to some chemicals?
column2:
Delayed elimination from a low-protein compartment. Amniotic fluid can act as a third distribution compartment with delayed elimination and low protein concentration.

PDF p. 265

column1: What alcohol-exposure advice does the source give for pregnancy?
column2:
Advise abstinence from alcohol exposure. The source advises abstinence and notes critical exposure can occur before the first missed period.

PDF p. 268

column1: How does maternal dilutional hypoalbuminemia alter xenobiotic handling?
column2:
It can increase the unbound biologically active fraction, changing placental transfer and clearance; total concentration alone may not describe active exposure.

PDF p. 265

column1: How do SGA and fetal growth restriction differ?
column2:
SGA describes size and does not by itself prove FGR. SGA is a size category; constitutionally small infants can be SGA, and FGR can occur above the tenth percentile.

PDF p. 276

column1: What common pathway causes fetal growth restriction?
column2:
Hypoxia and nutrient deprivation from placental insufficiency. Placental insufficiency limits fetal oxygen and nutrient delivery and is the commonest stated cause.

PDF p. 276

column1: What anthropometric pattern characterizes head-sparing FGR?
column2:
Asymmetric head-sparing restriction. Redistribution conserves delivery to brain and heart, producing relatively preserved head size and reduced weight or abdominal size.

PDF p. 278

column1: What information helps evaluate suspected growth restriction after birth?
column2:
Pregnancy trajectory, anthropometry, examination and placental findings. Prenatal pattern, maternal and family factors, physical findings and placental pathology can reveal the cause.

PDF p. 283

column1: Why are growth-restricted newborns vulnerable to hypoglycemia?
column2:
Limited glycogen and fat reserves with impaired gluconeogenesis. Reduced stores, impaired gluconeogenesis and sometimes limited ketone production increase vulnerability.

PDF p. 284

column1: Does fetal growth restriction guarantee accelerated functional lung maturity?
column2:
No. The source describes reduced lung growth, altered alveolar structure and pulmonary vascular dysfunction, with increased respiratory morbidity despite proposed stress-related maturation effects.

PDF p. 285

column1: What association helped establish the developmental-origins hypothesis?
column2:
Small birth size associated with later cardiometabolic disease. Replicated epidemiologic associations linked small birth size with later coronary disease, hypertension and metabolic disorders.

PDF p. 291

column1: Can adverse developmental programming occur without altered birth size?
column2:
Normal size does not exclude later programming effects. The source describes later disease after nutritional perturbations without a change in size and after several nonnutritional stresses.

PDF p. 291

column1: What does environmental mismatch mean in DOHaD?
column2:
Mismatch between early developmental cues and later environment. A larger disparity between early adaptation and the later environment can increase disease risk.

PDF p. 294

column1: How can epigenetic changes alter phenotype?
column2:
DNA or histone modification affecting gene regulation. Epigenetic modifications can link environmental exposures with stable changes in gene expression.

PDF p. 299

column1: What competing goals complicate postnatal nutritional planning?
column2:
Balance adequate brain energy with potential nutritional excess. The source emphasizes both adequate developing-brain nutrition and avoidance of excess, with long-term follow-up.

PDF p. 301

column1: What distinguishes an epidemiologic association from a deterministic prediction in developmental origins?
column2:
Population associations identify elevated risks and hypotheses; they do not establish that every exposed individual will develop a particular adult disease.

PDF p. 291

column1: Why is gestational hypertension a provisional diagnosis?
column2:
It may resolve, progress to preeclampsia or reveal chronic hypertension. The group includes transient disease, evolving preeclampsia and previously unrecognized chronic hypertension.

PDF p. 305

column1: What laboratory triad defines HELLP syndrome?
column2:
HELLP syndrome. HELLP denotes hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets; hypertension or proteinuria need not both be present.

PDF p. 307

column1: Why is surveillance needed even without initial severe preeclampsia features?
column2:
Progression may be unpredictable and rapid. Progression can occur within hours to days, and postpartum presentation is also possible.

PDF p. 311

column1: Which factors shape the decision to deliver in preeclampsia?
column2:
Gestational age, disease severity and maternal-fetal well-being. Delivery treats the maternal disease, but prematurity creates fetal risks; timing requires integrated assessment.

PDF p. 312

column1: Why is magnesium sulfate used in severe preeclampsia?
column2:
Prevention of eclamptic seizures. Magnesium sulfate is supported for seizure prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia.

PDF p. 313

column1: What longer-term follow-up issue follows a history of preeclampsia?
column2:
An increased later cardiovascular risk supports ongoing surveillance and prevention; the association does not resolve whether shared risks or preeclampsia itself drive all of the excess risk.

PDF p. 308

column1: How do pregestational and gestational diabetes differ in timing?
column2:
Pregestational diabetes. Pregestational diabetes precedes conception; gestational diabetes is recognized during pregnancy.

PDF p. 322

column1: What limitation of risk-factor-only GDM screening does the source describe?
column2:
Many affected patients have no identified risk factor. The source describes substantial missed cases among women without historical risk factors.

PDF p. 322

column1: Why does glucose control before conception matter for anomaly prevention?
column2:
Organogenesis occurs early, often before later pregnancy treatment begins. The relevant malformation window is early organogenesis, so preconception control is important.

PDF p. 325

column1: Why can an infant of a diabetic mother become hypoglycemic after delivery?
column2:
Persistent increased insulin after maternal glucose supply stops. Insulin production remains upregulated after separation from the maternal nutrient source.

PDF p. 328

column1: Why does a history of GDM require postpartum follow-up?
column2:
Future diabetes risk remains and glucose reassessment is needed. Insulin needs often fall postpartum, but impaired glucose metabolism and later type 2 diabetes remain important risks.

PDF p. 327

column1: What symptoms can accompany hypoglycemia in infants of diabetic mothers?
column2:
Infants may be asymptomatic or have tremor, seizures, poor feeding, respiratory distress or hypotonia, supporting glucose monitoring rather than reliance on symptoms alone.

PDF p. 328

column1: What gestational boundary defines preterm delivery in the source?
column2:
Preterm because it precedes37 weeks. The source defines preterm delivery as occurring before 37 completed weeks, within its stated lower gestational boundary.

PDF p. 333

column1: What is tertiary prevention in the chapter’s framework?
column2:
Tertiary intervention. Tertiary measures aim to improve outcomes for preterm infants.

PDF p. 333

column1: Why does the source advise against routine bed rest for threatened preterm labor?
column2:
Benefit is unproven and adverse effects are possible. The source finds no demonstrated benefit and cites thromboembolism, weakness, bone loss and depression as harms.

PDF p. 344

column1: What is the main practical goal of short-term tocolysis in the source?
column2:
Gain time for corticosteroids, neuroprotection or transfer. The goal has shifted toward a short window, often48 hours, for beneficial interventions and transport.

PDF p. 348

column1: Which neonatal benefits are supported for antenatal corticosteroids?
column2:
Antenatal glucocorticoids. Trials and meta-analysis show reduced RDS, neonatal mortality, IVH and NEC with antenatal glucocorticoids.

PDF p. 357

column1: Why is reviewing a previous spontaneous preterm birth history useful?
column2:
It helps identify recurrent and potentially modifiable risks and informs surveillance alongside accurate gestational dating and current findings.

PDF p. 343

column1: Which maternal immunoglobulin class crosses the placenta?
column2:
IgG. Maternal IgG crosses the placenta, unlike IgM and IgA in the source’s description.

PDF p. 367

column1: How does fetal-neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia develop?
column2:
Maternal IgG against a fetal platelet alloantigen. Maternal sensitization to an antigen-positive fetus produces IgG that crosses back and destroys fetal platelets.

PDF p. 369

column1: Can FNAIT occur in a first pregnancy?
column2:
A first pregnancy does not exclude FNAIT. The source reports that many FNAIT cases occur during the first pregnancy of at-risk couples.

PDF p. 369

column1: Should treatment of clinically suspected serious FNAIT wait for complete immunologic testing?
column2:
Start indicated management on clinical suspicion without waiting for the workup. The source states that suspected cases should be treated based on clinical diagnosis, with management shaped by count, bleeding and risk.

PDF p. 369

column1: Which maternal antibodies are emphasized in neonatal lupus?
column2:
Anti-Ro and anti-La. The source focuses on anti-Ro and anti-La in neonatal lupus.

PDF p. 371

column1: Why may the mother be clinically disease-free in an alloimmune fetal disorder?
column2:
The maternal immune response targets an exogenous fetal antigen rather than necessarily injuring maternal tissue.

PDF p. 367

column1: How do dizygotic twins arise?
column2:
Two sperm fertilize two ova. Dizygotic twins result from two separate fertilizations; monozygotic twins arise from early cleavage of one conceptus.

PDF p. 376

column1: Why is early determination of chorionicity important?
column2:
Chorionicity. Accurate early chorionicity determination guides pregnancy-specific follow-up and risk assessment.

PDF p. 377

column1: What fluid pattern is typical of TTTS?
column2:
Unbalanced volume transfer through placental anastomoses. Donor hypovolemia produces oliguria and oligohydramnios; recipient overload produces polyuria and polyhydramnios.

PDF p. 379

column1: What distinguishes TAPS from the principal imbalance in TTTS?
column2:
Twin anemia-polycythemia sequence. TAPS is characterized by donor anemia and recipient polycythemia, unlike the principal volume imbalance of TTTS.

PDF p. 382

column1: Why is the pump twin at risk in TRAP sequence?
column2:
Heart failure from supplying both circulations. The pump twin supports both fetuses through placental connections and may develop congestive heart failure.

PDF p. 382

column1: Why are monoamniotic twins vulnerable to cord entanglement?
column2:
Both cords occupy the same amniotic sac, so entanglement can be demonstrable from early pregnancy.

PDF p. 383

column1: At what gestation is a pregnancy post-term in this source?
column2:
Post-term. Post-term begins at 42 completed weeks or294 days from the last menstrual period.

PDF p. 388

column1: Why does first-trimester ultrasound improve gestational dating?
column2:
First-trimester ultrasound. Early ultrasound improves dating relative to menstrual recall and later pregnancy biometry.

PDF p. 388

column1: Why can post-term oligohydramnios lead to variable decelerations?
column2:
Umbilical cord compression. Reduced fluid increases vulnerability to cord compression and associated fetal heart rate abnormalities.

PDF p. 390

column1: What external findings characterize the described postmaturity syndrome?
column2:
Postmaturity syndrome. The classic syndrome includes absent vernix, dry cracked skin and an alert, aged appearance.

PDF p. 390

column1: Which cervical features favor successful induction?
column2:
A more dilated and effaced cervix. A favorable cervix, engaged presenting part and parity are associated with greater success.

PDF p. 391

column1: Why can live-birth registries underestimate the total mortality burden of prolonged pregnancy?
column2:
They exclude intrauterine fetal deaths, so their denominator and case capture do not describe all perinatal losses.

PDF p. 390

column1: What distribution of excess fetal fluid supports hydrops fetalis?
column2:
Excess fluid in multiple fetal compartments consistent with hydrops. The source defines hydrops by excessive fluid in at least two listed spaces or compartments.

PDF p. 396

column1: How can maternal Rh antibodies cause fetal disease?
column2:
Maternal antibodies cross the placenta and hemolyze fetal erythrocytes. Maternal anti-Rh antibodies can cross the placenta and cause fetal red-cell destruction.

PDF p. 396

column1: What initial laboratory information supports prevention and evaluation of alloimmunization?
column2:
ABO group, RhD status and antibody screen. The source recommends blood grouping, RhD determination and antibody screening alongside relevant history.

PDF p. 398

column1: Which Doppler measurement is used to assess risk of fetal anemia?
column2:
Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity. Serial MCA peak systolic velocity assessment replaced older serial amniotic bilirubin approaches for anemia surveillance.

PDF p. 400

column1: Which physiologic disturbances can cause nonimmune hydrops?
column2:
Reduced lymphatic return, reduced oncotic pressure or increased venous pressure. Imbalance of interstitial production and lymphatic return can arise through several pressure and drainage disturbances.

PDF p. 404

column1: What components help identify the cause of nonimmune hydrops?
column2:
Detailed personal/family history, targeted ultrasound, fetal echocardiography, MCA Doppler, laboratory and viral evaluation, with genetic or invasive testing when appropriate.

PDF p. 405

column1: What protective and developmental functions does amniotic fluid provide?
column2:
Cushion fetus and cord while permitting movement and structural development. Fluid protects against trauma and permits mobility needed for growth and development.

PDF p. 411

column1: Why can severe fetal renal dysfunction cause oligohydramnios?
column2:
Loss of the major fetal urinary contribution. Fetal renal output is a fundamental source of fluid, especially in the second half of pregnancy.

PDF p. 411

column1: Why are amniotic fluid volumes usually estimated by ultrasound?
column2:
Direct measurement and dye dilution are cumbersome or invasive. Direct measurement is largely limited to cesarean delivery, and dye dilution requires invasive sampling and laboratory support.

PDF p. 412

column1: What caution follows comparisons of AFI with single deepest pocket?
column2:
More abnormal labels do not by themselves demonstrate better outcomes. The source describes more oligohydramnios diagnoses and interventions with AFI without improved perinatal outcome in these comparisons.

PDF p. 413

column1: How can impaired fetal swallowing cause polyhydramnios?
column2:
Reduced absorption/removal of amniotic fluid. Reduced fetal swallowing limits fluid removal and can produce polyhydramnios; overproduction and idiopathic cases also occur.

PDF p. 423

column1: Which broad factors determine management of oligohydramnios?
column2:
Severity, underlying cause and gestational age; a volume label alone does not specify a universal intervention.

PDF p. 422

column1: What is the most common route to intra-amniotic infection?
column2:
Ascension from the lower maternal genital tract. Most cases result from ascending bacteria; procedural and hematogenous routes occur less often.

PDF p. 429

column1: Does negative amniotic fluid culture exclude all intra-amniotic inflammation?
column2:
Fastidious microbes or sterile intra-amniotic inflammation. Negative cultures may reflect recovery limitations or sterile inflammation, so inflammation and infection are not identical labels.

PDF p. 429

column1: What limitation affects clinical diagnostic criteria for chorioamnionitis?
column2:
Individual signs have variable sensitivity and generally low specificity. Clinical criteria are often used because definitive sampling is unavailable, but their specificity is limited.

PDF p. 430

column1: Is chorioamnionitis alone a sufficient indication for cesarean delivery?
column2:
Infection alone does not justify cesarean delivery. No neonatal benefit from cesarean solely for chorioamnionitis is established, and maternal surgical complications may increase.

PDF p. 434

column1: Why should the obstetric fever assessment be communicated to neonatology?
column2:
The diagnosis, level of suspicion and rationale for maternal management. The source calls for conveying the diagnosis and management rationale so neonatal decisions reflect actual suspicion.

PDF p. 434

column1: Why should outcomes attributed to chorioamnionitis be interpreted cautiously?
column2:
Maternal fever has multiple causes, and clinical infection, microbiologic findings and histologic inflammation do not perfectly agree.

PDF p. 435

column1: What clinically useful information can placental examination provide?
column2:
Placental examination. Placental findings can identify infection risk, explain adverse outcomes and inform recurrence assessment.

PDF p. 440

column1: How can placental pathology be reviewed when the specimen cannot accompany a transferred infant?
column2:
Request referring-hospital slides and pathology report. Slides and reports can be requested for review by the receiving pathologist.

PDF p. 440

column1: How can maternal arterial stenosis affect the placenta?
column2:
Maternal vascular malperfusion. Stenosis of maternal arteries supplying the intervillous space produces maternal vascular malperfusion patterns.

PDF p. 443

column1: What protects fetal umbilical vessels from compression?
column2:
Hydrated extracellular matrix called Wharton jelly. Wharton jelly is a hydrated matrix protecting the fetal cord vessels.

PDF p. 443

column1: Does acute chorioamnionitis prove that the newborn is septic?
column2:
It is relevant infection-risk evidence but does not prove neonatal sepsis. The source notes that few infants are septic at birth despite acute chorioamnionitis, consistent with placental protection.

PDF p. 444

column1: What makes a suspected cord obstruction lesion more convincing pathologically?
column2:
Local injury at the proposed obstruction and downstream changes indicating materially compromised flow strengthen its significance.

PDF p. 443

column1: How do predominant pain mechanisms change across labor stages?
column2:
Visceral predominance first, somatic predominance second. First-stage cervical and lower uterine distention is predominantly visceral; pelvic and perineal distention adds somatic pain in the second stage.

PDF p. 448

column1: What factors influence fetal exposure to maternal analgesic drugs?
column2:
Consider placental transfer plus drug properties, dose and route. Lipid barrier crossing suggests transfer potential, while pharmacokinetics, dose and administration affect actual fetal exposure.

PDF p. 450

column1: Why can neuraxial local anesthetic cause hypotension?
column2:
Sympathetic blockade causes vasodilation and may reduce uteroplacental perfusion. Local-anesthetic sympathetic blockade causes vasodilation; persistent hypotension can impair uteroplacental flow.

PDF p. 457

column1: When is a pudendal block commonly used in obstetric care?
column2:
Pudendal block. Pudendal block may provide late-stage labor analgesia, particularly for forceps delivery.

PDF p. 455

column1: Which compartment receives medication in a spinal or intrathecal injection?
column2:
Subarachnoid/intrathecal space. Intrathecal and subarachnoid are terms for the spinal injection technique described.

PDF p. 456

column1: Why can dilute epidural local anesthetic with small opioid doses limit fetal systemic exposure?
column2:
It can provide effective neuraxial analgesia with low maternal systemic drug levels and therefore limited fetal exposure, according to the source.

PDF p. 457

column1: What should the immediate delivery-room newborn survey assess?
column2:
Breathing, color and a brief whole-body search for major anomalies or injury. The primary survey checks transition, major anomalies and birth injuries across the body.

PDF p. 467

column1: When should the detailed routine newborn examination occur in a well infant?
column2:
Perform the detailed examination within 24 hours while allowing the initial contact and feed. The source recommends routine examination within 24 hours while protecting at least the first hour and initial breastfeeding in well dyads.

PDF p. 467

column1: How can examination order be adapted when a newborn is quiet?
column2:
Listen to the heart and perform suitable quiet-state assessments while ensuring eventual whole-body examination. The sequence is flexible; heart, eyes, pulses and gentle hip assessment can take advantage of a quiet state.

PDF p. 468

column1: What should follow an abnormal newborn red reflex?
column2:
Direct ophthalmology consultation. An abnormal reflex can indicate serious ocular disease and warrants direct ophthalmologic assessment.

PDF p. 473

column1: Why can duct-dependent heart disease escape the first examination?
column2:
A patent ductus and high right-sided pressure can mask important disease. Hemodynamic transition may delay murmurs or symptoms until ductal closure and pressure changes occur.

PDF p. 475

column1: How should newborn growth percentiles be interpreted?
column2:
Use gestation-specific charts at birth; charts representing40-week newborns can misclassify late-preterm or postmature infants.

PDF p. 469

column1: Which events are included in the source definition of birth injury?
column2:
An injury sustained during labor or delivery. The source defines birth injury around labor and delivery and excludes prenatal procedure and neonatal resuscitation injuries.

PDF p. 489

column1: What is caput succedaneum?
column2:
Caput succedaneum. Caput is an edematous swelling over the presenting part of the scalp.

PDF p. 491

column1: In which tissue plane does a cephalhematoma lie?
column2:
Cephalhematoma. A cephalhematoma is a subperiosteal cranial blood collection.

PDF p. 492

column1: Where does a subgaleal hemorrhage accumulate?
column2:
Subgaleal hemorrhage. Subgaleal hemorrhage occupies the space beneath the galea and above the periosteum and is associated with instrumental delivery.

PDF p. 493

column1: Which bone is most frequently fractured during labor and delivery?
column2:
Clavicle. The chapter identifies the clavicle as the most frequently fractured bone during labor and delivery.

PDF p. 500

column1: Which complication warrants follow-up in neonatal subcutaneous fat necrosis?
column2:
Hypercalcemia can develop and requires prompt recognition to prevent neurologic and renal sequelae.

PDF p. 491

column1: Does congenital mean genetic?
column2:
The feature is present at birth, with genetic or nongenetic causes possible. Congenital denotes presence at birth; it does not specify cause.

PDF p. 518

column1: What distinguishes a major anomaly from a minor anomaly in the source?
column2:
Major anomaly. Major anomalies have significant surgical or cosmetic implications; minor anomalies do not have that significance.

PDF p. 518

column1: Why should multiple minor anomalies prompt a careful pattern search?
column2:
Look for a characteristic pattern and associated major malformations. Minor findings may be normal variants but combinations can identify patterns or associated major anomalies.

PDF p. 523

column1: What family-history approach supports evaluation of congenital anomalies?
column2:
A detailed three- to four-generation pedigree including losses and consanguinity. The source recommends a multigeneration pedigree with affected relatives, pregnancy losses and possible parental relatedness.

PDF p. 525

column1: Why can parental samples help interpret a neonatal copy-number variant?
column2:
Whether it is de novo or inherited, alongside phenotype assessment. Microarray can identify variants not responsible for the phenotype; inheritance information aids interpretation.

PDF p. 538

column1: What prenatal information should be reviewed in a newborn anomaly evaluation?
column2:
Pregnancy course, timed maternal illnesses and exposures, fetal movement and prenatal ultrasound, screening and diagnostic genetic results.

PDF p. 525

column1: What resuscitation capability should be present at every delivery in the source?
column2:
An individual responsible for the infant and capable of initiating PPV. Unexpected neonatal depression occurs; the source calls for a trained person whose primary responsibility is the infant.

PDF p. 543

column1: Which organ takes over primary gas exchange at birth?
column2:
Aerated lungs with increased pulmonary perfusion. The lungs replace the placenta as the primary gas-exchange organ and must receive pulmonary blood flow.

PDF p. 545

column1: Why should indicated resuscitation begin before the one-minute Apgar score?
column2:
Begin indicated support based on breathing and heart rate without waiting for Apgar scoring. Waiting for the score delays therapy; Apgar describes the infant’s state at specified times.

PDF p. 551

column1: Does a vigorous infant born through clear fluid require routine suctioning?
column2:
No routine suctioning is necessary. Routine suction is unnecessary in this setting; posterior pharyngeal stimulation may provoke bradycardia.

PDF p. 554

column1: What should follow initial stimulation if the infant remains apneic?
column2:
Prompt positive-pressure ventilation. Failure to respond should prompt PPV; ongoing ineffective stimulation delays ventilation and may worsen hypoxia.

PDF p. 554

column1: Why are very preterm infants at high risk of heat loss during initial stabilization?
column2:
They have a high surface-area-to-mass ratio, limited brown fat and immature thermal defenses; preplanned thermal measures and temperature monitoring are needed.

PDF p. 554

column1: Why is establishing functional residual capacity central to newborn transition?
column2:
Replacement of lung liquid by air and establishment of FRC. Lung aeration and FRC support gas exchange while pulmonary blood flow increases.

PDF p. 558

column1: Which positive-pressure device can function without an external gas supply?
column2:
Self-inflating bag. Self-inflating bags re-expand after compression and can operate without a gas supply.

PDF p. 561

column1: How does a T-piece device switch between peak inflation and PEEP/CPAP?
column2:
Occlude the T-piece opening. Occluding the opening delivers set peak pressure; leaving it open permits PEEP or CPAP.

PDF p. 562

column1: What facial area should a newborn resuscitation mask cover?
column2:
Mouth and nose without covering eyes or extending beyond the chin. Correct size and positioning over mouth and nose help limit leaks; eyes and chin should not be overlapped.

PDF p. 563

column1: Why does PEEP help maintain preterm lung volume?
column2:
Maintain end-expiratory volume and reduce distal airway collapse. PEEP helps maintain FRC and reduces end-expiratory collapse; physiologic rationale does not prove every clinical outcome.

PDF p. 568

column1: What can a respiratory function monitor add during mask ventilation?
column2:
It can help assess mask leak and delivered tidal volume, which clinicians may estimate inaccurately by observation alone.

PDF p. 564

column1: How does hypoxia impair ATP-dependent cell function?
column2:
Failure of ion pumps with sodium and calcium accumulation. ATP depletion impairs ion pumps, causing swelling, calcium accumulation and vulnerability to oxidative damage.

PDF p. 572

column1: How can reoxygenation after hypoxia generate reactive oxygen species?
column2:
Free-radical production during purine metabolism. Reintroduced oxygen permits xanthine-oxidase metabolism that generates ROS, illustrating reoxygenation injury.

PDF p. 572

column1: What cellular targets can ROS and reactive nitrogen species damage?
column2:
Membrane lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. Reactive species can peroxidize lipids and damage proteins, enzymes and nucleic acids.

PDF p. 572

column1: Why should saturation be interpreted against time after birth?
column2:
Normal transitional saturations change over the first minutes and vary with gestation. Healthy infants in the observational datasets required minutes to reach high saturations, with slower stabilization in preterm infants.

PDF p. 578

column1: Where was preductal pulse oximetry placed for the cited saturation nomogram?
column2:
Right wrist. The cited studies obtained preductal measurements at the right wrist.

PDF p. 578

column1: Why does very-preterm oxygen supplementation remain an area requiring careful interpretation of evidence?
column2:
These infants risk both prolonged hypoxemia and oxidative injury; the source describes conflicting trial findings and unresolved optimal initial oxygen strategies.

PDF p. 579

column1: Why is effective ventilation central in neonatal cardiovascular collapse?
column2:
Asphyxia from inadequate gas exchange. Asphyxia is the usual cause; establishing ventilation often avoids compressions and drugs.

PDF p. 582

column1: When are neonatal chest compressions indicated in the described algorithm?
column2:
Chest compressions coordinated with ventilation. Persistent severe bradycardia despite effective lung inflation is the compression indication described.

PDF p. 582

column1: How does epinephrine support coronary perfusion during neonatal CPR?
column2:
Raise aortic diastolic pressure to improve coronary perfusion. Coronary perfusion during CPR depends on the diastolic pressure gradient; epinephrine can improve that gradient.

PDF p. 585

column1: Does shock after asphyxia necessarily indicate hypovolemia?
column2:
Myocardial dysfunction may cause shock without low circulating volume. Most asphyxiated infants are not hypovolemic; reduced myocardial function and cardiac output can explain shock.

PDF p. 585

column1: What diagnosis should be considered after sudden deterioration during initially effective ventilation?
column2:
Pneumothorax impairing venous return. A large pneumothorax can compress venous return, reduce output and cause hypotension and bradycardia.

PDF p. 590

column1: Why should complex resuscitations be documented and debriefed?
column2:
Accurate event recording and deliberate team discussion identify improvements in preparation, communication and technical performance for rare high-stakes events.

PDF p. 582

column1: How does delaying cord clamping change placental blood distribution?
column2:
More placental blood can return to the infant. Delay permits placental transfusion and reduces residual placental blood volume.

PDF p. 595

column1: Which preterm benefits are supported for delayed cord clamping in the source?
column2:
Reduced hospital mortality and fewer blood transfusions. The source reports reduced mortality, higher hematocrit and reduced transfusion needs.

PDF p. 595

column1: What later hematologic benefit is described after delayed clamping in term infants?
column2:
Iron-deficiency anemia. Placental transfusion improves early hemoglobin and hematocrit and reduces later infant iron-deficiency anemia.

PDF p. 595

column1: How do intact and cut-cord milking differ?
column2:
Intact cord milking. Intact milking uses the attached uncut cord with repeated refilling; cut-cord milking uses a detached segment.

PDF p. 598

column1: What risk signal limits cord milking in extremely preterm infants?
column2:
Higher severe IVH risk with milking than delayed clamping in extremely preterm infants. The source cites severe-IVH concerns in23–27-week infants and warns against extrapolating one strategy to another.

PDF p. 598

column1: Why is cord management in nonvigorous newborns particularly uncertain in this edition?
column2:
Many trials excluded these infants or did not separately report them, and possible transfusion benefit must be weighed against timely resuscitation.

PDF p. 599

column1: What are the four modes of neonatal heat exchange?
column2:
Convection, radiation, evaporation and conduction. All four heat-exchange modes vary with maturity, environment and postnatal age.

PDF p. 605

column1: Why is evaporative heat loss especially high in extremely preterm infants?
column2:
An immature skin barrier. Skin barrier competence develops with maturity, so very immature infants have much higher transepidermal water and heat loss.

PDF p. 605

column1: What defines the thermoneutral zone?
column2:
The range allowing normal temperature at minimal metabolic rate using nonevaporative adjustments. Thermoneutrality includes metabolic efficiency; a normal temperature alone does not prove it.

PDF p. 607

column1: How does increased ambient humidity affect evaporative heat loss?
column2:
Increase appropriate incubator humidity. Higher humidity lowers evaporative loss and can aid fluid and heat balance in very immature infants.

PDF p. 610

column1: What thermal hazard can follow skin-servo probe detachment?
column2:
Overwarming from inappropriate heat delivery. A detached probe can lead to overwarming; device readings must be interpreted alongside infant assessment.

PDF p. 610

column1: How does skin maturation change thermal requirements after very preterm birth?
column2:
As the barrier matures over days and weeks, evaporative loss falls, so the environment required for thermal balance changes and should be reassessed.

PDF p. 605

column1: Why can NICU experiences influence preterm neurodevelopment?
column2:
Physical and social experiences can modify developing neural connections. Rapid growth, synaptogenesis and plasticity make care experiences capable of supporting or disrupting development.

PDF p. 615

column1: Why may a preterm infant’s sleep be called indeterminate?
column2:
Indeterminate sleep. Immature sleep states may not meet established REM or NREM criteria and can be classified as indeterminate.

PDF p. 616

column1: How does parent-infant skin-to-skin contact support neonatal care?
column2:
Coregulation of infant physiology and behavior. The source describes physiologic, behavioral, thermal and breastfeeding benefits of supported skin-to-skin contact.

PDF p. 618

column1: Does a weak behavioral pain response mean an extremely preterm infant cannot feel pain?
column2:
Pain sensitivity remains despite immature behavioral expression. Very preterm infants are pain-sensitive despite weak overt responses; repeated pain is associated with developmental effects.

PDF p. 621

column1: Which NICU design features support milk expression and breastfeeding?
column2:
Privacy, accessible pumps, comfortable chairs and convenient milk storage. Practical design and valuing breastfeeding as interaction support expression and feeding opportunities.

PDF p. 622

column1: Why is infection prevention also a neurodevelopmental concern in the NICU?
column2:
Sepsis is associated with increased death or cerebral palsy risk; care routines and environmental design that reduce infection also support development.

PDF p. 623

column1: Why does monitor training matter beyond attaching a sensor?
column2:
Recognize device function, artifact and true physiologic events. The source emphasizes safe accurate acquisition and user understanding to avoid nuisance alarms and distortion of real events.

PDF p. 631

column1: Why should repeated ECG probe applications be minimized in very immature infants?
column2:
Skin injury and increased transepidermal water loss. Repeated applications can impair adhesion and signal and injure fragile skin, increasing water loss.

PDF p. 631

column1: What happens if an arterial pressure transducer is too high relative to the heart?
column2:
An erroneously low blood-pressure reading. Incorrect elevation can lower the displayed arterial pressure; proper leveling and zeroing are required.

PDF p. 632

column1: What feature helps pulse oximetry estimate arterial saturation?
column2:
Heartbeat-related pulsatile light absorption. Ratios of pulsatile to constant red and infrared signals estimate the fraction of oxygenated arterial hemoglobin.

PDF p. 634

column1: Why can sidestream capnography underestimate CO2 in very small preterm infants?
column2:
Constant aspiration of expired gas relative to small available volumes. Sampling requirements can be problematic at very low tidal volumes; microstream approaches use smaller samples.

PDF p. 637

column1: Why should transcutaneous CO2 values be interpreted with awareness of arterial agreement?
column2:
The relationship varies with perfusion, skin metabolism, electrode temperature and CO2 level, so displayed values are not universally interchangeable with arterial measurements.

PDF p. 637

column1: What common clinical questions do neonatal chest and abdominal radiographs address?
column2:
Device position, acute thoracoabdominal disease and treatment response. Radiographs assess support-device placement, urgent conditions and response to interventions.

PDF p. 643

column1: What materials commonly limit ultrasound transmission?
column2:
Sound transmits poorly through air and calcified structures. Air and calcified structures restrict sonographic windows; operator skill and probe choice also matter.

PDF p. 645

column1: What radiographic pattern commonly accompanies neonatal surfactant-deficient RDS?
column2:
Surfactant-deficient RDS. Alveolar collapse produces the characteristic low-volume granular or ground-glass appearance.

PDF p. 648

column1: Which radiographic and temporal pattern supports transient tachypnea?
column2:
Transient tachypnea from retained lung fluid. TTN is a clinical diagnosis with nonspecific retained-fluid appearances and usually a benign resolving course.

PDF p. 650

column1: Does a normal abdominal radiograph exclude malrotation in a newborn with bilious vomiting?
column2:
Continue urgent evaluation for malrotation or volvulus when no other cause is defined. Malrotation can have a normal radiograph; bilious vomiting is a potential surgical emergency requiring appropriate evaluation.

PDF p. 656

column1: What neonatal MRI precautions remain relevant even when sedation can be avoided?
column2:
Use MRI-safe monitoring and equipment, prevent hypothermia and maintain appropriate observation; feed-and-swaddle techniques can avoid sedation in many young infants.

PDF p. 645

column1: Why does neonatal anesthesia require developmental expertise?
column2:
Immature organ systems and altered drug handling. Anatomy, physiology, homeostasis and pharmacology differ between adults, term neonates and preterm neonates.

PDF p. 674

column1: Which neonatal airway proportions matter during airway planning?
column2:
Relatively large head and tongue with a short neck and higher anterior larynx. Neonatal proportions affect positioning and airway management; these differences extend beyond size.

PDF p. 682

column1: Why does a fall in heart rate threaten neonatal cardiac output?
column2:
Limited ability to augment stroke volume. The neonatal heart has limited stroke-volume reserve, making cardiac output strongly dependent on heart rate.

PDF p. 683

column1: How does anesthesia increase neonatal heat-loss risk?
column2:
Blunted thermoregulation plus cutaneous vasodilation. Anesthesia interferes with thermal defenses and increases heat loss; open cavities add risk.

PDF p. 684

column1: Why can hypoglycemia be missed during neonatal anesthesia?
column2:
Limited reserves and masked clinical signs under anesthesia. Neonates have high glucose demand and limited reserves, while anesthesia masks usual signs.

PDF p. 684

column1: Why may a very small sick preterm infant need prolonged postoperative respiratory support?
column2:
Immature clearance prolongs anesthetic effects, illness and prematurity complicate emergence, and hypothermia can prolong neuromuscular blockade; ongoing NICU care may be needed.

PDF p. 693

column1: Why are many periviable care practices not supported by large randomized trials?
column2:
Many trials excluded periviable infants, so some practice rests on accumulated experience. The chapter presents Japanese experience and notes frequent trial exclusion of infants below 24 weeks.

PDF p. 696

column1: Why should survival and neurodevelopment be discussed separately in periviable counseling?
column2:
Improved survival does not imply absence of later impairment. The source reports progress in survival alongside persistent developmental morbidity, requiring separate outcome discussion.

PDF p. 696

column1: Why should dating accuracy be checked before periviable counseling?
column2:
Review the accuracy and uncertainty of gestational dating. Outcomes vary within the periviable period and ultrasound dating retains uncertainty, making accuracy relevant to counseling.

PDF p. 697

column1: Which losses inform fluid planning for a periviable infant?
column2:
Adjust to individual insensible loss, urine output and weight trends while avoiding overload. The source emphasizes substantial losses despite humidity and the risks associated with fluid overload.

PDF p. 701

column1: What role does functional echocardiography play in the described periviable care approach?
column2:
Functional echocardiography. The approach emphasizes functional echocardiographic assessment of cardiovascular function to inform circulatory management.

PDF p. 703

column1: Why can the most immature myocardium respond poorly to preload and afterload changes?
column2:
Immature calcium handling, myocardial structure and contractile/diastolic function limit adaptation and produce a relatively flat Frank-Starling response.

PDF p. 704

column1: What gestational ages define late preterm birth?
column2:
Late preterm. Late preterm spans 34 weeks through 36 weeks 6 days; size does not establish maturity.

PDF p. 713

column1: Why can late preterm infants struggle to transfer milk?
column2:
Immature suck-swallow-breathe coordination and endurance. Neurologic and oral-motor immaturity can make feeding ineffective despite mature appearance.

PDF p. 718

column1: What clearance process contributes to respiratory transition after birth?
column2:
Immaturity of epithelial sodium-mediated fluid absorption. The chapter links epithelial sodium transport, labor-related signals and maturation to lung liquid clearance.

PDF p. 719

column1: Why do late preterm infants need careful bilirubin follow-up?
column2:
Increased risk of important hyperbilirubinemia after discharge. Late preterm bilirubin handling and feeding vulnerabilities increase jaundice and readmission risk.

PDF p. 723

column1: What feeding evidence is sought before discharge in the source pathway?
column2:
Continue assessment until successful feeding is documented. The pathway requires successful feeding with coordinated sucking, swallowing and breathing, alongside other readiness criteria.

PDF p. 725

column1: What follow-up interval does the source recommend after late preterm discharge?
column2:
Arrange a physician visit within 24–48 hours after discharge, with feeding, jaundice and caregiver readiness assessed in the discharge plan.

PDF p. 726

column1: What is the physiologic purpose of trophic feeding?
column2:
Stimulate intestinal structural and functional maturation. Small volumes provide intestinal stimulation; the chapter also notes uncertainty in trial outcomes and optimal duration.

PDF p. 735

column1: Should gastric residuals alone stop feeds in an otherwise well infant?
column2:
Residual volume alone does not justify stopping feeds. The chapter finds no evidence supporting discontinuation solely for residuals in the absence of other symptoms.

PDF p. 735

column1: What milk alternative is recommended when mother’s own milk is unavailable?
column2:
Pasteurized donor human milk with attention to nutrient adequacy. Pasteurized donor milk is recommended; fortification and growth monitoring address compositional differences.

PDF p. 739

column1: Why is human milk fortified for many premature infants?
column2:
Milk alone may not supply enough protein and minerals for preterm needs. Preterm requirements can exceed milk supplies of protein, calcium, phosphorus and other nutrients; fortification improves growth.

PDF p. 739

column1: Why should fortifier comparisons be interpreted cautiously in this edition?
column2:
Further direct comparisons are needed before declaring one fortifier superior. The chapter distinguishes the trial’s primary PN-duration outcome from secondary findings and calls for well-designed head-to-head trials.

PDF p. 739

column1: How does milk protein content change during lactation, and why does that matter?
column2:
Protein content declines over the first weeks. Fixed assumptions about baseline milk composition can overestimate delivered protein, particularly with donor milk.

PDF p. 740

column1: What benefits can skin-to-skin care offer stabilized preterm infants and parents?
column2:
Supported skin-to-skin contact. Skin-to-skin care supports attachment and breastfeeding and can promote infant physiologic stability.

PDF p. 753

column1: How should clinicians communicate a newborn’s course to families?
column2:
Explain in straightforward language and coach participation. Warm, clear communication and coaching help parents understand and participate in care.

PDF p. 754

column1: What does a positive Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale screen require?
column2:
Further evaluation is warranted. A positive screen identifies need for evaluation and referral rather than supplying a final diagnosis.

PDF p. 755

column1: How should suspected postpartum psychosis be handled?
column2:
Urgent psychiatric evaluation with infant safety prioritized. Suspected postpartum psychosis warrants emergency referral; rapid fluctuation and risks to parent and infant demand safety planning.

PDF p. 756

column1: How can discharge planning reduce parental anxiety?
column2:
Skills training and supported rooming-in before discharge. Sustained planning, practical skills and rooming-in can build confidence for home care.

PDF p. 758

column1: Why should reduced NICU visitation prompt exploration rather than a judgment about bonding?
column2:
Visitation may reflect parental depression, distress or practical barriers. Sensitive assessment and support are needed rather than inferring lack of concern.

PDF p. 755

column1: What is the central purpose of perinatal palliative care?
column2:
Optimize comfort and quality of life while supporting family decisions. Palliative care coordinates multidisciplinary support for infant comfort and caregiver needs throughout the decision process.

PDF p. 761

column1: Which NICU groups can benefit from palliative care?
column2:
Palliative assessment of benefits, burdens and family goals. The chapter includes long-suffering NICU patients, extreme prematurity and life-limiting diagnoses among potential beneficiaries.

PDF p. 762

column1: Are perinatal resuscitation preferences necessarily all-or-none and permanent?
column2:
Define a treatment trial and revisit goals as response becomes known. The source describes a spectrum of interventions and opportunities to reassess clinical response and goals.

PDF p. 765

column1: Which nonpharmacologic measures can support neonatal comfort?
column2:
Holding, swaddling and non-nutritive sucking. Simple noninvasive measures may reduce distress and continue as adjuncts when medication is required.

PDF p. 767

column1: What is the therapeutic goal when treating end-of-life dyspnea?
column2:
Relieve dyspnea using the comfort plan, including appropriate opioids. For end-of-life dyspnea the goal is comfort; opioids are described as a mainstay of symptom relief.

PDF p. 769

column1: What should clinicians discuss when a desired resuscitative intervention may be technically impossible?
column2:
Discuss feasibility and alternatives antenatally when anticipated, and revisit goals as the infant’s condition and response become clearer.

PDF p. 765

column1: Which drug properties favor placental diffusion?
column2:
Small, lipid-soluble, largely unionized and weakly protein-bound. These properties favor movement across placental membranes by passive diffusion.

PDF p. 776

column1: How does neonatal body water affect hydrophilic drug distribution?
column2:
A larger volume of distribution per kilogram. Newborns have relatively more total and extracellular body water, increasing distribution of hydrophilic drugs.

PDF p. 781

column1: Which drug fraction is pharmacologically active?
column2:
The unbound pharmacologically active fraction. Reduced binding increases the fraction available to exert pharmacologic effects; total adult ranges need cautious interpretation.

PDF p. 781

column1: Which slowly developing enzyme contributes to prolonged caffeine half-life?
column2:
Delayed CYP1A2 activity. The primary caffeine demethylation pathway involves CYP1A2, which develops slowly after birth.

PDF p. 782

column1: How can indomethacin affect clearance of a filtration-dependent drug?
column2:
Reduced renal perfusion can decrease gentamicin clearance. Prostaglandin inhibition can increase renal vascular resistance and reduce clearance of filtration-dependent drugs.

PDF p. 783

column1: Why must neonatal drug regimens be reassessed as an infant matures?
column2:
Gestational and postnatal maturation alter distribution, hepatic metabolism and renal elimination, often changing required doses or intervals; efficacy and tolerability still require monitoring.

PDF p. 784

column1: Why may weak bases accumulate in breast milk?
column2:
Ion trapping in milk that is slightly more acidic than plasma. A unionized weak base can cross the membrane and become ionized in milk, limiting diffusion back.

PDF p. 787

column1: How is relative infant dose calculated?
column2:
Relative infant dose expressed as a percentage. RID divides weight-adjusted infant dose by weight-adjusted maternal dose and expresses the ratio as percent.

PDF p. 788

column1: Why does drug presence in milk not necessarily imply substantial systemic exposure?
column2:
Low infant oral bioavailability. The ingested drug must be absorbed to cause systemic effects; local intestinal effects and infant-specific uncertainty still matter.

PDF p. 788

column1: Which infant findings warrant attention with maternal opioid analgesia?
column2:
Possible opioid-related sedation or lethargy. Infants can be sensitive to opioid exposure; selection, lowest effective dose, duration and clinical monitoring matter.

PDF p. 790

column1: What monitoring is advised during longer-term maternal medication treatment?
column2:
Choose an appropriate agent and monitor infant activity and growth. The chapter recommends individualized selection, minimizing effective exposure and monitoring the infant during long-term therapy.

PDF p. 791

column1: Why is a single milk-to-plasma ratio an imperfect exposure measure?
column2:
It assumes simultaneous blood and milk concentrations are at equilibrium; changing concentrations and infant milk intake can make that snapshot misleading.

PDF p. 787

column1: What is constant during first-order elimination?
column2:
A constant fraction eliminated per unit time. First-order elimination removes a constant proportion over time, producing an exponential concentration decrease.

PDF p. 798

column1: How can hydrops affect hydrophilic drug distribution?
column2:
An expanded volume of distribution. Excess extracellular fluid can expand the distribution space for hydrophilic drugs.

PDF p. 800

column1: Why can normal early creatinine be misleading in acute kidney injury?
column2:
Renal clearance may already be reduced before creatinine rises. Creatinine takes time to accumulate, so falling filtration can precede a measurable rise.

PDF p. 800

column1: Why can cooling and rewarming require dose reassessment?
column2:
Monitor exposure when available and reassess through cooling and rewarming. Temperature, perfusion and recovery of organ function can change exposure over the treatment course.

PDF p. 801

column1: Which exposure feature is particularly important for beta-lactam efficacy?
column2:
Time above MIC during the dosing interval. Beta-lactam efficacy is associated with the duration that concentrations exceed the MIC.

PDF p. 804

column1: What does AUC measure in pharmacokinetics?
column2:
The area under the concentration-time curve reflects total drug exposure over the measured interval.

PDF p. 803

column1: Which symptom domains predominate in neonatal opioid withdrawal?
column2:
CNS irritability, autonomic overactivity and gastrointestinal dysfunction. Opioid receptor distribution in the nervous system and gut helps explain the clinical domains.

PDF p. 814

column1: Why should an exposure history not end the diagnostic evaluation?
column2:
Consider infection and metabolic or neurologic causes as well. Withdrawal can mimic infection, glucose or calcium disturbances and neurologic injury; concurrent causes need consideration.

PDF p. 815

column1: Why can a urine drug screen miss prenatal exposure?
column2:
Rapid elimination can make urine testing miss earlier exposure. Many drugs clear rapidly; specimen type and timing determine the detection window.

PDF p. 815

column1: What are important nonpharmacologic measures for an infant at risk of withdrawal?
column2:
Reduce stimuli, swaddle, comfort and support frequent appropriate feeds. Supportive care targets comfort, nutrition, sleep and growth while watching for dehydration and weight loss.

PDF p. 817

column1: What is the source’s goal when medication is needed for withdrawal?
column2:
Reduce signs to a tolerable level while restoring function. The chapter emphasizes function and short-term symptom reduction; it does not establish long-term benefit from drug treatment.

PDF p. 817

column1: How does maternal maintenance treatment affect breastfeeding considerations in this source?
column2:
When the mother adheres to supervised methadone or buprenorphine treatment and has no other contraindication, breastfeeding can be encouraged with infant growth and clinical monitoring.

PDF p. 817

column1: Which immunoglobulin class is actively transported across placenta?
column2:
IgG. Placental Fc receptors actively transport maternal IgG, especially late in pregnancy.

PDF p. 856

column1: What may elevated cord IgM indicate?
column2:
Fetal antigen exposure and antibody synthesis, while considering maternal-fetal bleeding. IgM does not normally cross placenta; elevation can reflect fetal synthesis, but total IgM is not pathogen-specific and bleeding can complicate interpretation.

PDF p. 856

column1: Which complement pathways can activate without specific antibody?
column2:
Alternative and lectin pathways. Alternative activation can occur on surfaces and lectin activation follows recognition of microbial carbohydrates.

PDF p. 834

column1: Which antibody predominates in human milk?
column2:
Secretory IgA. Secretory IgA predominates and its secretory component supports resistance to gastrointestinal digestion.

PDF p. 857

column1: What infection patterns raise concern for a host-defense defect?
column2:
An immune defect alongside other predisposing conditions. Unusual, recurrent or incompletely treated infections and associated growth problems warrant investigation of host defenses.

PDF p. 858

column1: How does lactoferrin contribute to antimicrobial protection in milk?
column2:
It binds iron, limiting availability of a growth cofactor to susceptible bacteria.

PDF p. 858

column1: Why does neonatal blood-culture volume matter?
column2:
Low specimen volume can miss low-level bacteremia. The chapter emphasizes sufficient volume to improve detection when organism concentrations are low.

PDF p. 864

column1: Does a negative blood culture rule out neonatal meningitis?
column2:
Blood results alone should not determine whether CSF evaluation is needed. Blood and CSF cultures correlate imperfectly; lumbar puncture is considered according to suspicion and stability.

PDF p. 864

column1: What population limitation does this edition give for the EOS calculator?
column2:
The cited tool is validated for infants at least 35 weeks, not this population. The source limits validation to at least 35 weeks and emphasizes local incidence and clinical monitoring.

PDF p. 865

column1: When does the source support stopping empiric antibiotics in a well infant with negative cultures?
column2:
Discontinue empiric antibiotics after clinical reassessment. The source describes stopping at 36–48 hours in well infants without evidence of infection, while separating more uncertain symptomatic cases.

PDF p. 867

column1: How should urine for definitive neonatal UTI culture be obtained?
column2:
Catheterized urine or suprapubic bladder aspirate. Catheterization or suprapubic aspiration reduces the contamination problem of bag collections.

PDF p. 871

column1: What findings suggest omphalitis extending beyond uncomplicated local infection?
column2:
Abdominal-wall involvement, black eschar or extensive edema should prompt consideration of necrotizing fasciitis; systemic illness requires urgent assessment and treatment.

PDF p. 874

column1: Which cultures matter in evaluating invasive neonatal candidiasis?
column2:
Blood, urine and CSF cultures as clinically appropriate. Sterile-site cultures remain central; urine and CSF may reveal infection not shown by blood culture.

PDF p. 892

column1: Can normal CSF counts exclude neonatal fungal CNS infection?
column2:
CSF culture still matters because routine indices may be normal. CNS candidiasis can occur without candidemia and without abnormal routine CSF chemistries or counts.

PDF p. 896

column1: Why does catheter removal matter during Candida bloodstream infection?
column2:
Prompt removal of the implicated central catheter when feasible. Prompt removal is associated with improved clearance and outcomes; Candida biofilms can resist drug penetration.

PDF p. 900

column1: What should persistent candidemia prompt clinicians to investigate?
column2:
Look for infected thrombi and end-organ abscesses. Persistent candidemia increases concern for dissemination, including catheter-tip thrombi and abdominal or brain foci.

PDF p. 893

column1: How do gestational timing and severity relate in congenital toxoplasmosis?
column2:
Transmission rises later, while earlier fetal infection tends to be more severe. The probability of transmission and severity move in different directions with gestation.

PDF p. 917

column1: What exposure routes transmit Toxoplasma to humans?
column2:
Ingesting tissue cysts in raw or poorly cooked meat, or oocysts from contaminated food or water, including contamination associated with cat feces.

PDF p. 916

column1: Does absence of vesicles exclude disseminated neonatal HSV?
column2:
Disseminated herpes simplex infection. Disseminated HSV can involve liver and lungs and may occur without skin vesicles.

PDF p. 924

column1: Why is CSF HSV PCR useful?
column2:
CSF HSV PCR. PCR is especially valuable because CSF viral culture has low recovery; blood PCR alone does not classify disease extent.

PDF p. 925

column1: By what age must CMV be identified to establish congenital infection in this source?
column2:
Identification within the first 21 days. Early identification is necessary because later positivity may reflect perinatal acquisition.

PDF p. 934

column1: What birth intervention does the source describe for an infant of an HBsAg-positive mother?
column2:
Hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG at separate sites within 12 hours. Active vaccine and passive immunoglobulin provide complementary protection after known maternal infection.

PDF p. 958

column1: How can parvovirus B19 produce fetal hydrops?
column2:
Infection of erythroid precursors causing impaired red-cell production. Erythroid maturation arrest can cause profound anemia and high-output cardiac failure with hydrops.

PDF p. 961

column1: Why can HSV serology be difficult to interpret in newborns?
column2:
