Transplacentally transferred maternal antibodies confound interpretation; virologic tests from appropriate sites are more useful for neonatal diagnosis.

PDF p. 925

column1: What is neurulation?
column2:
Modeling, folding and closure into the neural tube. Neurulation includes plate formation, modeling, groove formation and closure.

PDF p. 984

column1: What does inside-out cortical lamination mean?
column2:
Later neurons occupy progressively more superficial layers. After early deep layers form, later neurons pass them toward superficial cortical positions.

PDF p. 987

column1: What role do radial glia play in cortical development?
column2:
Guidance of radial neuronal migration. Radial glia provide scaffolding for migrating cortical neurons and help preserve topographic organization.

PDF p. 988

column1: Which cells produce central nervous system myelin?
column2:
Oligodendrocytes. Oligodendrocytes mature through defined stages to become myelinating cells.

PDF p. 1000

column1: How do agyria and pachygyria differ?
column2:
Agyria and pachygyria, respectively. Agyria is lack of gyration; pachygyria describes reduced broad gyri with shallow sulci in the lissencephaly spectrum.

PDF p. 1008

column1: Why does a genetic explanation not exclude environmental influence on brain development?
column2:
Genes and prenatal or postnatal environments interact to regulate proliferation, migration, maturation and circuit formation; malformations can reflect either or both.

PDF p. 984

column1: Which glial developmental process is impaired in diffuse white matter injury?
column2:
Injury and arrested maturation of pre-oligodendrocytes. Diffuse injury includes impaired oligodendrocyte maturation and broader developmental effects.

PDF p. 1016

column1: What does a two-hit model propose for encephalopathy of prematurity?
column2:
An early exposure can increase susceptibility to later injury. The model considers interactions among temporally separated insults within a multifactorial process.

PDF p. 1018

column1: What white matter injury can be missed by ultrasound?
column2:
Diffuse white matter injury is not excluded. Ultrasound detects cystic PVL well but has limited sensitivity for diffuse noncystic injury.

PDF p. 1023

column1: How may ADC change during acute white matter injury?
column2:
Reduced water mobility associated with cellular and axonal swelling. Acute cytotoxic and axonal swelling can lower ADC before conventional changes become clear.

PDF p. 1025

column1: Does DEHSI alone establish major developmental impairment?
column2:
The isolated signal finding does not establish significant developmental delay. The source distinguishes DEHSI alone from combinations including white matter loss and stresses limitations of prediction.

PDF p. 1025

column1: Why is encephalopathy of prematurity broader than focal PVL?
column2:
It includes diffuse white matter injury, neuronal and axonal involvement and altered maturation of interconnected gray and white matter systems.

PDF p. 1016

column1: Where does germinal matrix hemorrhage commonly originate?
column2:
Caudothalamic germinal matrix. The germinal matrix around the caudate is a common origin in preterm infants.

PDF p. 1038

column1: Why are serial ultrasound studies useful after GMH-IVH?
column2:
Serial cranial ultrasound to assess evolution and ventricular dilatation. Serial ultrasound permits detection, grading and monitoring of posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation.

PDF p. 1037

column1: Which hemorrhage pattern in a term infant raises concern for cerebral sinovenous thrombosis?
column2:
Cerebral sinovenous thrombosis. The chapter highlights IVH with or without unilateral thalamic hemorrhage as a possible CSVT presentation.

PDF p. 1037

column1: How can perinatal arterial ischemic stroke present?
column2:
Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke. PAIS often presents with focal clonic seizures and warrants appropriate neuroimaging.

PDF p. 1037

column1: How should long-term risk after low-grade IVH be framed?
column2:
Studies differ; grade alone does not determine an individual outcome. The source reviews conflicting low-grade outcome studies and potential contributions of accompanying injury.

PDF p. 1049

column1: How does lesion location affect outcomes after periventricular hemorrhagic infarction?
column2:
Different sites disrupt different motor, visual and cognitive pathways; lesion size and location help inform targeted follow-up and rehabilitation rather than relying on grade alone.

PDF p. 1050

column1: Why is there an early therapeutic window after hypoxic-ischemic injury?
column2:
Secondary mitochondrial energy failure and delayed cell injury can follow the initial insult. The source describes delayed energy failure after the initial insult, supporting early assessment and intervention.

PDF p. 1066

column1: What is the role of modified Sarnat assessment early after birth?
column2:
Structured grading of encephalopathy using the modified Sarnat approach. Modified clinical scoring supports assessment within the early cooling decision window.

PDF p. 1063

column1: Within what postnatal window were infants cooled in the cited trials?
column2:
Initiation within 6 hours of birth. The cited trials began hypothermia within 6 hours and demonstrated reduced death or severe disability in eligible mature infants.

PDF p. 1082

column1: Which seizures may be missed by limited-channel aEEG?
column2:
Brief, low-amplitude or focal seizures may be missed. The chapter supports raw EEG review and conventional EEG because limited-channel displays can miss events.

PDF p. 1072

column1: Why should one early Apgar score not be used alone for long-term prognosis?
column2:
Integrate serial examination, EEG, imaging and treatment context. Early Apgar scores have limited long-term predictive sensitivity; hypothermia also changes interpretation of older prognostic data.

PDF p. 1084

column1: Why monitor and correct glucose disturbances after an asphyxial insult?
column2:
Hypoglycemia can add to injury in an already vulnerable brain; metabolic support is part of systemic and brain-oriented care.

PDF p. 1080

column1: Why is EEG important even when no convulsions are visible?
column2:
Electrographic-only seizures can occur without visible signs. A large proportion of neonatal seizures are electrographic-only and require monitoring for recognition.

PDF p. 1096

column1: Which features favor jitteriness over clonic seizure?
column2:
Jitteriness, with assessment for underlying causes. Stimulus sensitivity and suppressibility favor jitteriness; hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia and other causes still need consideration.

PDF p. 1096

column1: What pattern supports benign neonatal sleep myoclonus?
column2:
Benign neonatal sleep myoclonus. Sleep restriction, cessation with arousal and no ictal correlate support the benign sleep-related phenomenon.

PDF p. 1097

column1: What is electroclinical dissociation after treatment?
column2:
Suppression of visible activity without termination of electrical seizures. Antiseizure medication can suppress the motor component while cortical electrical activity persists.

PDF p. 1096

column1: How should adequacy of neonatal antiseizure treatment be assessed?
column2:
EEG assessment of electrical seizure activity. The source identifies elimination of electrical seizure activity as the therapeutic endpoint because clinical observation is unreliable.

PDF p. 1108

column1: Why should neonatal seizure evaluation investigate etiology as well as treat events?
column2:
Hypoxic-ischemic injury, stroke, hemorrhage, infection and metabolic disturbances can require specific investigation and treatment; an antiseizure response does not identify the cause.

PDF p. 1097

column1: What should be considered before classifying hypotonia as a primary neuromuscular disorder?
column2:
Assess acute systemic illness, metabolic disturbance and medication exposure. Many acute or multisystem illnesses and maternal medications can reduce tone.

PDF p. 1121

column1: What general pattern favors a central cause of hypotonia?
column2:
Central hypotonia with less weakness than the degree of low tone. Central causes often reduce tone disproportionately to weakness; exceptions require full assessment.

PDF p. 1121

column1: What pattern of weakness is described in infantile spinal muscular atrophy?
column2:
Anterior horn cell degeneration. Infantile SMA affects spinal anterior horn cells and lower brainstem motor nuclei.

PDF p. 1123

column1: Which maternal history can clarify severe neonatal weakness with facial diplegia?
column2:
Congenital myotonic dystrophy. The congenital form of DM1 is usually maternally inherited; maternal examination and molecular testing support diagnosis.

PDF p. 1130

column1: What enzyme defect causes infantile Pompe disease?
column2:
Acid alpha-glucosidase. Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency produces lysosomal glycogen accumulation involving muscle and heart.

PDF p. 1133

column1: Why does absence of clinical myotonia not exclude congenital myotonic dystrophy?
column2:
Neonatal clinical and electrical myotonia may be absent and develop later; severe weakness, facial features and maternal findings can be more informative at birth.

PDF p. 1130

column1: How should head circumference be measured and interpreted?
column2:
Measure maximal occipitofrontal circumference and plot on an age-appropriate preterm chart. Consistent occipitofrontal measurement and age-adjusted growth charts help assess intracranial growth.

PDF p. 1136

column1: What makes a full anterior fontanelle more concerning?
column2:
Consider an intracranial process with increased pressure. Sustained bulging can indicate raised intracranial pressure; crying-related transient fullness is different.

PDF p. 1136

column1: Does macrocephaly always mean hydrocephalus?
column2:
Enlarged brain, abnormal intracranial structures or hydrocephalus. The chapter distinguishes increased brain volume, masses or vascular lesions, and enlarged CSF spaces.

PDF p. 1138

column1: How does a fused cranial suture alter skull growth?
column2:
Restricted growth perpendicular to the fused suture with compensatory growth elsewhere. Failure of perpendicular growth and compensation at unfused sites produce characteristic patterns.

PDF p. 1143

column1: Which ear displacement favors positional plagiocephaly?
column2:
Positional plagiocephaly. Forward ipsilateral ear displacement and a parallelogram pattern favor positional deformity; lambdoid synostosis tends to displace the ear posteriorly.

PDF p. 1145

column1: Why should head assessment include both size and shape?
column2:
Circumference tracks intracranial growth, while shape and suture examination can reveal positional deformation or premature suture fusion even without a striking size abnormality.

PDF p. 1136

column1: How does a meningocele differ from a myelomeningocele?
column2:
Meningocele. In meningocele, meninges herniate but the spinal cord and roots remain within the canal.

PDF p. 1150

column1: Can closed spinal dysraphism cause later neurologic compromise?
column2:
Closed dysraphism can tether neural tissue despite intact skin. Closed lesions include lipomyelomeningocele and other tethering disorders.

PDF p. 1150

column1: Which lumbosacral findings increase concern for occult dysraphism?
column2:
Investigate for underlying dysraphism; these are concerning stigmata. Multiple stigmata, lipomas and dermal sinuses are higher-risk findings in the source framework.

PDF p. 1152

column1: Why does spinal ultrasound become less informative as infants age?
column2:
Ossification of posterior elements reduces the ultrasound window. MRI offers detailed soft-tissue anatomy as ossification limits ultrasound access.

PDF p. 1153

column1: What is an immediate management priority for open spinal dysraphism?
column2:
Protect the lesion with sterile covering and coordinate prompt specialist management. Exposed neural tissue and CSF create infection risk; sterile protection, indicated antimicrobial care and surgical coordination are central.

PDF p. 1154

column1: What does the two-hit hypothesis propose for myelomeningocele?
column2:
Initial failure of closure is followed by additional injury from intrauterine exposure, pressure or trauma; fetal repair aims to reduce this second component in selected cases.

PDF p. 1156

column1: What do otoacoustic emissions primarily assess?
column2:
Outer hair cells. OAE reflects outer hair-cell function; outer or middle-ear obstruction can interfere with measurement.

PDF p. 1159

column1: Why can an infant pass OAE but fail ABR?
column2:
Neural hearing loss with preserved outer hair-cell function. OAE can miss neural disease involving inner hair cells, auditory nerve or brainstem pathways.

PDF p. 1159

column1: Does failing the newborn hearing screen prove permanent hearing loss?
column2:
Arrange timely follow-up because transient conductive interference can cause failure. A screening result requires follow-up; transient outer or middle-ear dysfunction can cause false-positive failure.

PDF p. 1159

column1: When should early intervention referral occur after confirmed hearing loss?
column2:
Refer to early intervention at diagnosis, including unilateral loss. Early individualized family-centered services are recommended for unilateral and bilateral hearing loss.

PDF p. 1161

column1: Why continue hearing and language surveillance after a passed newborn screen?
column2:
Audiologic and speech-language assessment because delayed or progressive loss can occur. Mild loss may be missed and some causes, including CMV, can produce delayed or progressive hearing loss.

PDF p. 1165

column1: What role does genetics evaluation have after confirmed infant hearing loss?
column2:
Families should be offered evaluation and counseling to investigate cause, associated disorders, prognosis and recurrence considerations.

PDF p. 1163

column1: What should the first follow-up after NICU discharge assess?
column2:
Home adaptation, medication and oxygen administration, feeding preparation and parental concerns. Early visits assess safe practical care and emerging medical or developmental needs.

PDF p. 1179

column1: What can a General Movement Assessment help identify?
column2:
Prechtl General Movement Assessment for neuromotor risk. General movement quality can help identify risk of neuromotor deficits, including spastic cerebral palsy.

PDF p. 1180

column1: Why can early infant testing underestimate later difficulties?
column2:
Higher-level demands can expose difficulties not captured by early developmental tests. Early assessments emphasize different skills; subtle cognitive, behavioral and coordination problems may emerge later.

PDF p. 1182

column1: Why compare participants lost to follow-up with those retained?
column2:
Attrition may bias the observed outcome rates. Differential dropout can change the apparent risk and limits generalizability.

PDF p. 1182

column1: Why should a positive autism screen in a preterm child receive contextual evaluation?
column2:
Further evaluation should consider coexisting impairments and the full developmental profile. The source notes substantial coexisting disability among screen-positive preterm children; screening supports evaluation rather than replacing it.

PDF p. 1184

column1: What domains can early intervention after prematurity address?
column2:
Parent education and relationships, infant development, and individualized physical, occupational, speech or educational therapies according to identified needs.

PDF p. 1186

column1: During which stage does most airway branching occur?
column2:
Pseudoglandular stage. The pseudoglandular stage establishes the branching airway pattern and associated vascular pathways.

PDF p. 1193

column1: Which changes make gas exchange increasingly possible in the canalicular lung?
column2:
Acinar formation, thinning air-blood barrier and emerging type II-cell surfactant synthesis. Airspace and vascular approximation plus epithelial differentiation begin to establish gas-exchange capacity.

PDF p. 1193

column1: What do lamellar bodies in developing type II cells signify?
column2:
Surfactant storage and secretion. Lamellar bodies are characteristic organelles of surfactant-producing type II epithelial cells.

PDF p. 1195

column1: What epithelial transport helps clear lung liquid after birth?
column2:
Sodium absorption through epithelial sodium channels. Active sodium transport promotes absorption; developmental and labor-related signals influence the transition from secretion to clearance.

PDF p. 1198

column1: How does surfactant support alveolar stability?
column2:
Higher surface tension promotes collapse and heterogeneous expansion. Low surface tension helps prevent alveolar collapse and fluid entry; deficiency produces uneven recruitment and overdistention.

PDF p. 1204

column1: What developmental pattern can chronic preterm lung injury produce?
column2:
Interrupted alveolarization and vascular development can yield fewer, larger alveoli and attenuated microvasculature, with less fibrosis than the classic older BPD pattern.

PDF p. 1196

column1: How does grunting help a distressed newborn maintain lung volume?
column2:
Expiratory braking that helps preserve functional residual capacity. Partial glottic closure retains gas and increases expiratory pressure; after intubation PEEP helps replace this mechanism.

PDF p. 1213

column1: How can alveolar overdistention worsen carbon dioxide elimination?
column2:
Increased dead space. Gas trapping and overdistention can increase ineffective ventilation and reduce CO2 elimination.

PDF p. 1215

column1: Why does pulse oximetry poorly distinguish degrees of hyperoxemia?
column2:
Large changes in PaO2 may produce little change in saturation. The flat upper dissociation curve limits discrimination of high arterial oxygen tensions.

PDF p. 1216

column1: What does respiratory compliance describe?
column2:
Compliance. Compliance relates volume change to pressure change; a stiffer system has lower compliance and greater elastance.

PDF p. 1219

column1: What determines a respiratory system time constant?
column2:
Their resistance-compliance products differ. The time constant reflects resistance multiplied by compliance, with heterogeneous mechanics affecting equilibration.

PDF p. 1222

column1: What fraction of a step change equilibrates after one time constant?
column2:
Approximately 63%; about five time constants allow approximately 99% equilibration in the simplified linear model.

PDF p. 1222

column1: How does surfactant deficiency produce respiratory distress?
column2:
Insufficient surfactant synthesis or secretion. Surfactant deficiency promotes collapse, hypoventilation and ventilation-perfusion imbalance; injury and protein leak can further inactivate surfactant.

PDF p. 1229

column1: Which antenatal treatment accelerates fetal lung maturation?
column2:
Antenatal corticosteroids. Antenatal corticosteroids induce developmentally regulated proteins and reduce incidence and severity of RDS in appropriate preterm-risk settings.

PDF p. 1231

column1: What is the classic radiographic pattern in preterm surfactant deficiency?
column2:
Low volumes, diffuse ground-glass pattern and air bronchograms. Diffuse atelectasis produces ground-glass opacity with aerated bronchi against poorly aerated alveoli.

PDF p. 1232

column1: What benefits does exogenous surfactant provide in RDS?
column2:
Reduced RDS mortality and pneumothorax risk, without guaranteed prevention of BPD. Surfactant replacement improves important acute outcomes; BPD remains multifactorial and can follow limited early RDS.

PDF p. 1233

column1: How does thin-catheter surfactant delivery differ from conventional intubation and ventilation?
column2:
LISA or MIST. LISA/MIST aims to deliver surfactant while preserving spontaneous breathing and CPAP support, limiting invasive ventilation exposure.

PDF p. 1234

column1: Why might surfactant response be less favorable than expected?
column2:
Severe disease or surfactant inactivation from inflammation, oxidant injury, hemorrhage or protein-rich edema can impair the response.

PDF p. 1233

column1: How does CPAP improve respiratory mechanics in an immature lung?
column2:
Maintenance of end-expiratory lung volume and airway patency. CPAP prevents end-expiratory collapse, supports FRC and can stent the upper airway.

PDF p. 1242

column1: What is the purpose of hybrid volume-targeted ventilation?
column2:
Keep tidal volume within a target range despite changing mechanics. Hybrid systems use feedback to adjust delivery toward a volume target; neonatal leaks and measurement limitations still matter.

PDF p. 1253

column1: Why can a short expiratory time cause inadvertent PEEP?
column2:
Gas trapping with incomplete exhalation. Insufficient time relative to the resistance-compliance time constant leaves gas behind and can cause overinflation.

PDF p. 1250

column1: What ventilated-infant pattern suggests tension pneumothorax?
column2:
Tension pneumothorax. Pleural air under pressure can impair ventilation and circulation and requires prompt treatment.

PDF p. 1266

column1: How do volutrauma and atelectrauma differ?
column2:
Volutrauma and atelectrauma, respectively. Volutrauma is overdistention injury; atelectrauma follows repetitive recruitment and derecruitment.

PDF p. 1267

column1: Why must support be reassessed when lung compliance improves?
column2:
A given pressure can deliver a larger tidal volume as compliance improves; volume and gas-exchange monitoring help avoid unintended overventilation and overdistention.

PDF p. 1253

column1: Why can respiratory failure persist beyond lung compression in diaphragmatic hernia?
column2:
Pulmonary hypoplasia with abnormal vascular development. Both lungs can have reduced airspace and vascular development, particularly on the involved side, with increased vascular resistance.

PDF p. 1275

column1: Must neonatal chylous fluid be milky before feeds begin?
column2:
Clear fluid does not exclude chylothorax before enteral feeding. Chylous fluid becomes characteristically milky with established feeding; fluid analysis helps diagnosis.

PDF p. 1279

column1: What blood-supply finding helps identify pulmonary sequestration?
column2:
Bronchopulmonary sequestration. Systemic arterial supply is a distinguishing feature of sequestrated nonfunctioning lung tissue.

PDF p. 1282

column1: How can meconium aspiration impair surfactant function?
column2:
Inflammatory injury and alveolar protein leak can damage type II cells and inactivate surfactant. Aspiration injury combines obstruction, inflammation and impaired surfactant production or function.

PDF p. 1285

column1: What mechanism and time course characterize typical TTN?
column2:
Delayed clearance of fetal lung liquid. Typical TTN reflects delayed liquid absorption and usually resolves over the first days; early pneumonia and other causes can overlap.

PDF p. 1289

column1: Why should the early label TTN remain provisional in a symptomatic newborn?
column2:
Its early presentation can overlap with pneumonia and other respiratory disease; clinical course and appropriate evaluation are needed.

PDF p. 1289

column1: What differentiates central and obstructive apnea?
column2:
Obstructive apnea. Obstruction preserves effort against a closed airway; central apnea has absent respiratory effort.

PDF p. 1309

column1: Why can impedance monitoring miss obstructive events?
column2:
Chest movement does not establish airway patency or ventilation. Impedance monitoring detects movement and central pauses but can miss obstruction while effort continues.

PDF p. 1309

column1: What should a new increase in baseline apnea prompt?
column2:
Investigate infection, NEC and other new causes. New or increased apnea can signal sepsis or NEC and requires contextual assessment.

PDF p. 1313

column1: Should acid suppression routinely treat apnea of prematurity?
column2:
Do not routinely use acid suppression to treat apnea. Temporal linkage is uncommon and routine reflux treatment has not shown apnea benefit; acid suppression can add infectious and NEC risks.

PDF p. 1313

column1: Which receptor action contributes to caffeine’s respiratory stimulation?
column2:
Antagonism of adenosine receptors. Methylxanthines antagonize adenosine receptors and improve ventilation and responsiveness to carbon dioxide.

PDF p. 1314

column1: How does the neonatal hypoxic ventilatory response differ from the sustained adult response?
column2:
It is often biphasic: an initial rise in ventilation is followed by depression, particularly in preterm infants.

PDF p. 1307

column1: What symptom pattern suggests bilateral choanal obstruction?
column2:
Bilateral choanal atresia. Preferential nasal breathing makes bilateral posterior nasal obstruction particularly symptomatic; crying can allow oral airflow.

PDF p. 1320

column1: What is the most common cause of infant stridor in this source?
column2:
Laryngomalacia. Laryngomalacia produces dynamic supraglottic collapse and is the most common infant stridor cause; severe symptoms require further assessment.

PDF p. 1325

column1: What findings can accompany unilateral vocal-cord paralysis?
column2:
Unilateral vocal-cord paralysis with possible aspiration. Vocal-cord dysfunction can cause dysphonia and feeding-related aspiration symptoms; laryngoscopy can confirm mobility.

PDF p. 1327

column1: What airway lesion is associated with a beard-distribution hemangioma?
column2:
Subglottic infantile hemangioma. Segmental beard-distribution hemangioma can be associated with a subglottic vascular lesion requiring airway evaluation.

PDF p. 1328

column1: Why can formal operative assessment be needed for a laryngeal cleft?
column2:
Formal airway evaluation with palpation of the interarytenoid region. Swallow assessment and flexible laryngoscopy contribute, but definitive diagnosis requires formal evaluation and palpation.

PDF p. 1328

column1: Which features make laryngomalacia more concerning than uncomplicated intermittent stridor?
column2:
Constant stridor, increased work of breathing, apnea, failure to thrive or cardiopulmonary consequences indicate a more severe course requiring specialist assessment.

PDF p. 1326

column1: Why can BPD incidence vary with the definition used?
column2:
Definitions and local oxygen practices can change classification and predicted risk. BPD definitions evolved with treatment and survival; different criteria have limitations and can affect comparisons.

PDF p. 1332

column1: What pathologic pattern is typical of contemporary milder BPD?
column2:
Impaired alveolar and vascular development. Modern BPD often reflects arrested or disrupted development and reduced gas-exchange surface area.

PDF p. 1336

column1: Why monitor pulmonary hypertension in severe BPD?
column2:
Early echocardiographic assessment and prevention of hypoxemia. Pulmonary hypertension can complicate severe BPD; oxygenation during sleep, feeding and activity matters.

PDF p. 1342

column1: Why is growth monitoring central in BPD care?
column2:
Optimize nutrient density and monitor weight, length and head growth. Increased demand and interrupted feeding can impair growth; malnutrition can delay alveolar development and weaning.

PDF p. 1343

column1: How should chronic steroid use in established BPD be approached?
column2:
Use clearly defined goals after assessing benefits and adverse effects. Steroids can have short-term anti-inflammatory effects, but long-term respiratory outcomes in established BPD are not established and adverse effects matter.

PDF p. 1342

column1: Why does prevention of BPD require multiple strategies?
column2:
Prematurity, mechanical injury, oxygen exposure, inflammation and impaired vascular or alveolar development interact; one acute respiratory treatment does not address every pathway.

PDF p. 1339

column1: How can disrupted lung development contribute to later pulmonary hypertension?
column2:
Reduced alveolar-capillary growth with vascular dysfunction and remodeling. Reduced vessel number and abnormal growth interact with hypoxia, hypercarbia and other stressors to elevate vascular resistance.

PDF p. 1349

column1: Does absence of a measurable tricuspid-regurgitation jet exclude pulmonary hypertension?
column2:
Pulmonary hypertension is not excluded; assess other findings and the clinical picture. The chapter notes that absent measurable TRJV does not rule out pulmonary hypertension; other signs and longitudinal evaluation matter.

PDF p. 1349

column1: How can wheeze after preterm birth differ from typical allergic asthma?
column2:
Prematurity-related airway injury and altered development can contribute. Preterm wheezing phenotypes can differ from term allergic asthma and occur with or without BPD.

PDF p. 1351

column1: Why include preterm birth in an adult respiratory history?
column2:
Reduced lung growth and altered lifelong function after prematurity. Developmental lung impairment and subsequent exposures can influence the trajectory toward adult obstructive disease.

PDF p. 1353

column1: Why measure respiratory outcomes beyond NICU BPD status in trials?
column2:
Longer-term respiratory benefit still needs direct assessment. BPD or discharge support is not a sufficient surrogate for all postneonatal airway outcomes.

PDF p. 1352

column1: Why does the source describe optimal oxygen targets in postneonatal pulmonary hypertension as an evidence gap?
column2:
Guideline targets differ and have not been systematically studied in this specific population; source recommendations should be read with that limitation.

PDF p. 1349

column1: From which embryonic tissue do the bilateral heart fields arise?
column2:
Lateral plate mesoderm. Bilateral heart fields derived from lateral plate mesoderm contribute to the early tube.

PDF p. 1358

column1: What does dextral looping accomplish in the primitive heart?
column2:
Dextral looping. Looping repositions segments of the growing tube as chamber differentiation and septation proceed.

PDF p. 1358

column1: What is the role of endocardial cushions in heart development?
column2:
Cushions that contribute to valves and septa. Endothelial-mesenchymal transition populates cardiac jelly; cushions act as primitive valves and shape later septa and valves.

PDF p. 1363

column1: Which developmental structures receive important cardiac neural crest contributions?
column2:
Outflow septation and aortic arch artery development. Cardiac neural crest contributes to great-vessel walls, outflow septation and cardiac neural structures.

PDF p. 1365

column1: What does lineage tracing suggest about the origin of conduction tissue?
column2:
Specialized conducting myocardium can be recruited from myocardial precursors. The source describes specialized myocardium arising from unspecialized myocardial cells, with signaling influencing recruitment.

PDF p. 1367

column1: Why is coronary endothelial origin described cautiously in the epicardial discussion?
column2:
Different lineage-tracing approaches show several possible contributions and apparently conflicting patterns; the source presents an evolving account rather than one universally settled origin.

PDF p. 1367

column1: How does vasculogenesis differ from angiogenesis?
column2:
Vasculogenesis. Vasculogenesis forms vessels de novo from progenitors; angiogenesis extends existing vessels.

PDF p. 1372

column1: Why is high pulmonary vascular resistance physiologic before birth?
column2:
Placental gas exchange permits high pulmonary resistance and low lung flow. High fetal resistance directs blood through fetal channels while the placenta provides oxygenation.

PDF p. 1374

column1: Which two stimuli most strongly lower pulmonary resistance at birth?
column2:
A particularly large fall in pulmonary vascular resistance. Inflation and oxygenation independently lower resistance, with the greatest effects together; lung flow and pulmonary venous return increase.

PDF p. 1375

column1: How does nitric oxide relax pulmonary vascular smooth muscle?
column2:
Cyclic GMP. Nitric oxide activates soluble guanylate cyclase, increasing cGMP and promoting relaxation.

PDF p. 1376

column1: Why can disrupted vascular growth impair alveolarization?
column2:
Vascular and alveolar development are closely coupled. The chapter describes coordinated vascular and airway growth and experimental impairment of alveolarization after VEGF inhibition.

PDF p. 1373

column1: How does increased pulmonary venous return promote functional closure of the foramen ovale?
column2:
Increased lung flow raises pulmonary venous return and left atrial pressure, favoring functional closure as the postnatal circulations separate.

PDF p. 1375

column1: Why is a four-chamber view alone insufficient for fetal cardiac assessment?
column2:
Systematic segmental assessment including outflow tracts, arches and venous return. A fetal echocardiogram evaluates anatomy, connections, outflow tracts, arches and functional flow using two-dimensional and Doppler imaging.

PDF p. 1389

column1: Why can traditional high-risk referral alone miss many affected fetuses?
column2:
Many affected babies do not belong to these traditional high-risk groups. The chapter estimates that only a minority of affected babies would be identified by restricting echocardiography to traditional high-risk groups.

PDF p. 1389

column1: Which lesions may remain undetected despite an optimal fetal echocardiogram?
column2:
Small defects and minor valve abnormalities cannot be reliably excluded. Small structures are less readily assessed; small VSDs, partial anomalous pulmonary venous return and minor valve abnormalities may not be excluded.

PDF p. 1396

column1: How should prenatal cardiac findings influence the delivery plan?
column2:
Coordinate level of care, cardiology access, transport and likely intervention. Disease-specific findings permit risk-stratified delivery planning to prevent hemodynamic compromise.

PDF p. 1396

column1: What should counseling after fetal cardiac diagnosis include?
column2:
Reassess understanding and provide repeated empathetic counseling. Counseling includes findings, limitations, prognosis, management options and support, with understanding reassessed and sessions repeated as needed.

PDF p. 1396

column1: Why can atrial septal defects and patent ductus arteriosus not be ruled out prenatally?
column2:
Atrial and ductal communications are normal requirements of fetal circulation; persistence after birth cannot be determined simply from their prenatal presence.

PDF p. 1397

column1: Which postnatal changes favor ductal constriction?
column2:
Ductal smooth-muscle constriction. Oxygen promotes ductal contraction and falling PGE2 removes a relaxing influence; anatomic obliteration follows functional closure.

PDF p. 1401

column1: How does falling pulmonary resistance affect a persistent left-to-right ductal shunt?
column2:
Increasing pulmonary flow and left-heart volume load with possible systemic hypoperfusion. A persistent ductus permits increasing left-to-right shunting, pulmonary overflow and increased left-heart work as pulmonary resistance falls.

PDF p. 1402

column1: What does color Doppler echocardiography add to ductal assessment?
column2:
Color Doppler echocardiography. Echocardiography demonstrates patency, direction and velocity and evaluates pulmonary overflow and systemic hypoperfusion.

PDF p. 1403

column1: What systemic arterial Doppler pattern can accompany a large ductal shunt?
column2:
Evidence supporting systemic hypoperfusion from a large shunt. Absent or reversed systemic diastolic flow is one marker of systemic hypoperfusion, interpreted with the broader clinical and echocardiographic picture.

PDF p. 1403

column1: Why does successful ductal closure not itself prove improved long-term outcomes?
column2:
Trials demonstrating those patient-centered outcomes. The chapter emphasizes that randomized interventions often achieved closure without demonstrating the anticipated broader benefits.

PDF p. 1401

column1: What important immediate complication can follow surgical ductal ligation in a preterm infant?
column2:
Postligation left ventricular dysfunction with cardiorespiratory decompensation may require major escalation of support; reliable anatomic closure does not eliminate procedural risk.

PDF p. 1406

column1: Why is an adequate atrial communication important in dextro-transposition?
column2:
Parallel circulations require mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. The two circuits run in parallel; atrial mixing is particularly effective and may be essential to adequate systemic oxygenation.

PDF p. 1411

column1: Where do pulmonary veins drain in total anomalous pulmonary venous connection?
column2:
Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection. All pulmonary venous blood returns anomalously to the systemic venous circulation; variants depend on the level of drainage.

PDF p. 1416

column1: Why is systemic blood flow ductal dependent in hypoplastic left heart syndrome?
column2:
Loss of right-ventricular supply to the systemic circulation through the ductus. The right ventricle supplies systemic flow through the ductus, including retrograde arch and coronary flow; closure can cause profound hypoperfusion.

PDF p. 1419

column1: What bedside findings should raise concern for critical aortic coarctation?
column2:
Critical aortic coarctation. Critical arch obstruction can present with systemic hypoperfusion as ductal support disappears; pulse differences are important clues.

PDF p. 1423

column1: Why may a large ventricular septal defect become more symptomatic as pulmonary resistance falls?
column2:
Increasing left-to-right shunt as pulmonary resistance decreases. Falling pulmonary resistance promotes a larger left-to-right shunt and pulmonary overcirculation.

PDF p. 1425

column1: Why must congenital heart disease be assessed by physiology as well as anatomic labels?
column2:
The same anatomic category can have different flow limitations and mixing; physiology changes with falling pulmonary resistance and closure of fetal channels.

PDF p. 1430

column1: Does situs solitus guarantee normal atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial connections?
column2:
Normal visceral arrangement does not guarantee normal cardiac connections. Situs describes lateralization; concordance or discordance of cardiac connections requires separate evaluation.

PDF p. 1433

column1: What findings suggest a vein of Galen malformation in a neonate with heart failure?
column2:
Vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation. A large cerebral arteriovenous shunt can divert systemic flow and produce high-output failure, a bruit and hydrocephalus.

PDF p. 1436

column1: What course is described for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in infants of diabetic mothers?
column2:
Often resolves during the first six months. The chapter describes an excellent prognosis with complete resolution within the first six months for this specific form.

PDF p. 1441

column1: Why can a small rapidly developing effusion be dangerous?
column2:
Rapid accumulation causing cardiac tamponade. Rapid accumulation can raise intrapericardial pressure and impair filling even when fluid volume is small; central lines are a common iatrogenic cause.

PDF p. 1442

column1: What symptom combination should prompt consideration of a vascular ring?
column2:
Vascular ring or sling. Vascular rings may compress the airway and esophagus, producing combined respiratory and feeding symptoms.

PDF p. 1445

column1: Which imaging method best establishes pericardial effusion and its physiologic impact?
column2:
Echocardiography evaluates the fluid and its effects on chamber filling, including atrial or ventricular collapse and respiratory flow variation.

PDF p. 1442

column1: What is the treatment principle for sinus tachycardia?
column2:
Identify and treat the underlying cause. Sinus tachycardia is usually a response to conditions such as fever, infection or anemia; management targets the cause.

PDF p. 1453

column1: What baseline ECG features indicate a manifest accessory pathway?
column2:
Antegrade conduction over a manifest accessory pathway. Early ventricular activation through a manifest pathway produces pre-excitation; a concealed retrograde-only pathway has no baseline delta wave.

PDF p. 1456

column1: Why can ventricular rate be much slower than atrial rate during neonatal flutter?
column2:
Decremental atrioventricular nodal conduction. The AV node limits conduction of the rapid atrial rhythm, often in 2:1, 3:1 or 4:1 patterns.

PDF p. 1455

column1: What ECG sequence characterizes Mobitz type I block?
column2:
Mobitz type I second-degree block. Progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat is the Wenckebach pattern.

PDF p. 1465

column1: What must be checked before attributing a prolonged QT interval solely to congenital long QT syndrome?
column2:
Review QT-prolonging medicines and electrolyte disturbances. Medicines and hypocalcemia or hypokalemia may cause or exacerbate QT prolongation; both acquired and congenital forms can cause dangerous arrhythmias.

PDF p. 1467

column1: Why should very fast irregular atrial tachycardia prompt review of a central-line tip?
column2:
A catheter tip in the atrium can mechanically stimulate atrial tachycardia; line position should be assessed before assuming an intrinsic arrhythmia substrate.

PDF p. 1455

column1: What is the rationale for early prostaglandin E1 when ductal-dependent disease is suspected?
column2:
Promptly maintain ductal patency with prostaglandin E1 under monitoring. The chapter recommends prompt PGE1 while the diagnosis is confirmed because ductal flow may be lifesaving.

PDF p. 1490

column1: What is balloon atrial septostomy intended to improve?
column2:
Balloon atrial septostomy. Septostomy enlarges the atrial communication to improve mixing or atrial egress as required by the anatomy.

PDF p. 1482

column1: When can pulmonary artery banding be useful palliation?
column2:
Restrict pulmonary flow to improve circulatory balance. Banding is used selectively to limit pulmonary overcirculation, including some single-ventricle pathways.

PDF p. 1481

column1: Why can oxygen and ventilation strategies require special care in ductal-dependent single-ventricle physiology?
column2:
Changing pulmonary resistance can redistribute flow away from systemic perfusion. Single-ventricle output must supply both beds; lowering pulmonary resistance may increase pulmonary flow at the expense of systemic delivery.

PDF p. 1491

column1: Which effects of milrinone may assist a dysfunctional neonatal ventricle?
column2:
Inotropic, lusitropic and afterload-reducing effects. The combined effects can improve filling, stroke volume and output while reducing afterload.

PDF p. 1493

column1: Does most mild or moderate congenital heart disease require a special neonatal ventilation strategy?
column2:
Often standard neonatal strategies appropriate to age and size suffice; special resistance-balancing strategies depend on the specific physiology.

PDF p. 1491

column1: Why should neonatal coagulation results use age-appropriate reference ranges?
column2:
Developmental hemostasis differs from adults and requires neonatal interpretation. Several procoagulants and anticoagulants are lower in neonates; counterbalancing differences and age-specific ranges matter.

PDF p. 1499

column1: What is the mechanism of fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia?
column2:
Maternal IgG targeting fetal platelets bearing a paternal antigen. Transplacental maternal alloantibodies bind incompatible fetal platelet antigens and promote platelet clearance.

PDF p. 1503

column1: Which severe inherited factor deficiency may have normal PT and aPTT?
column2:
Factor XIII deficiency. Factor XIII deficiency is an exception in which routine PT and aPTT can remain normal; specific quantitative assays are needed.

PDF p. 1510

column1: Which screening test usually becomes abnormal first in vitamin K deficiency?
column2:
Isolated PT prolongation before aPTT prolongation. PT prolongation is the earliest screening abnormality, with aPTT prolongation as deficiency progresses.

PDF p. 1511

column1: How can disseminated intravascular coagulation produce both bleeding and organ injury?
column2:
Systemic coagulation activation with factor consumption and microvascular thrombosis. DIC combines coagulation and fibrinolytic activation, consumption of platelets and factors, and fibrin deposition that may impair organs.

PDF p. 1511

column1: Which triad suggests neonatal renal vein thrombosis?
column2:
Hematuria, a palpable flank mass and thrombocytopenia are cardinal clues; not every infant has all three, and Doppler ultrasonography confirms the diagnosis.

PDF p. 1513

column1: Why does erythropoietin fall after birth?
column2:
Higher tissue oxygenation suppresses erythropoietin production. Improved postnatal oxygenation lowers EPO and erythropoiesis, contributing to physiologic anemia.

PDF p. 1523

column1: Which initial tests help classify neonatal anemia?
column2:
CBC with indices, reticulocyte count and peripheral smear. Indices, reticulocytes and morphology guide the differential alongside history and examination.

PDF p. 1526

column1: What findings commonly support hemolysis rather than uncomplicated blood loss?
column2:
Accelerated red-cell destruction. Hemolysis commonly increases indirect bilirubin and LDH and stimulates reticulocytes; concurrent marrow suppression can blunt that response.

PDF p. 1530

column1: Why can maternal elevation of Hb F affect the Kleihauer-Betke test?
column2:
Maternal Hb F-containing cells can produce a false-positive result. The assay exploits acid resistance of Hb F-containing cells, so elevated maternal Hb F can confound results; flow cytometry may distinguish populations.

PDF p. 1530

column1: Why should specimen source be considered when assessing neonatal polycythemia?
column2:
Capillary values tend to exceed peripheral venous values. The chapter defines term polycythemia using peripheral venous values and notes higher capillary values; viscosity and clinical manifestations also matter.

PDF p. 1548

column1: Why does anemia of prematurity reach an earlier and often lower nadir than physiologic anemia in term infants?
column2:
Premature red cells have shorter survival and EPO remains low; illness and phlebotomy can add further losses or suppress production.

PDF p. 1523

column1: How should neutropenia be defined in a neonate?
column2:
An appropriate neonatal age and gestation reference distribution. Neonatal neutrophil values change rapidly and definitions depend on the relevant reference distribution.

PDF p. 1552

column1: What defect underlies chronic granulomatous disease?
column2:
NADPH oxidase dysfunction. CGD impairs oxidative microbial killing through defective NADPH oxidase in phagocytes.

PDF p. 1558

column1: What pattern suggests leukocyte adhesion deficiency?
column2:
Impaired neutrophil adhesion and migration into tissues. LAD impairs trafficking; neutrophils remain in blood rather than accumulating effectively at infected tissues.

PDF p. 1559

column1: Why is suspected severe combined immunodeficiency urgent?
column2:
Treat suspected severe combined immunodeficiency as an urgent specialist problem. SCID is described as a pediatric emergency; preserved B-cell numbers in some forms do not establish effective antibody function.

PDF p. 1560

column1: Which constellation should raise suspicion for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis?
column2:
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. HLH combines systemic inflammation, cytopenias and characteristic biochemical and immune abnormalities; neonatal cases are rare.

PDF p. 1563

column1: Does a normal or increased neutrophil count exclude a neutrophil functional defect?
column2:
No. CGD and leukocyte adhesion defects may present with normal or increased circulating counts while killing or tissue migration is impaired.

PDF p. 1559

column1: Which urine metabolites are commonly used in neuroblastoma assessment?
column2:
Homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid. Many neuroblastomas secrete catecholamines; urinary HVA and VMA are commonly used diagnostic tests.

PDF p. 1566

column1: Why does neonatal AFP require age-adjusted interpretation?
column2:
AFP is physiologically high at birth and must be assessed against age-appropriate values. Normal AFP is high at birth and declines over infancy; tumor assessment requires developmental context and the broader findings.

PDF p. 1567

column1: Which gene rearrangement is common in congenital and infant ALL and AML?
column2:
KMT2A. MLL is now described as KMT2A; rearrangements are common in congenital and infant acute leukemias.

PDF p. 1566

column1: Which fusion is associated with infantile fibrosarcoma?
column2:
ETV6-NTRK3. The source describes ETV6-NTRK3 in infantile fibrosarcoma and the relevance of TRK-directed therapy in selected settings.

PDF p. 1569

column1: What imaging modality is preferred for postnatal evaluation of a suspected neonatal brain tumor?
column2:
Magnetic resonance imaging. MRI defines the intracranial lesion for postnatal diagnosis and planning.

PDF p. 1569

column1: Why should a suspected inherited cancer predisposition prompt genetics input?
column2:
Different predisposition syndromes confer risks for specific tumors at particular developmental stages; genetics input informs family assessment and syndrome-specific surveillance.

PDF p. 1565

column1: Why are neonates particularly vulnerable to metabolic transfusion complications?
column2:
Immature handling of product solutes with a small circulating blood volume. Immature organ function and limited blood volume increase susceptibility to glucose, potassium and calcium disturbances.

PDF p. 1572

column1: Why can a large citrate load during exchange transfusion lower ionized calcium?
column2:
Citrate-associated calcium binding with limited neonatal citrate handling. Large citrate loads may cause symptomatic hypocalcemia, especially with immature metabolism; exchange differs from a small-volume transfusion.

PDF p. 1574

column1: Which blood-cell population carries latent CMV relevant to transfusion transmission?
column2:
Leukocytes. CMV remains latent in donor leukocytes and may be transmitted in cellular components; vulnerability is greatest in selected high-risk recipients.

PDF p. 1578

column1: What did the cited PlaNet-2 trial show about prophylactic platelet thresholds in preterm infants?
column2:
The higher-threshold group had more new major bleeding or death. In the cited premature-infant trial, the more liberal threshold was associated with more major bleeding or death; the result must be interpreted in its studied context.

PDF p. 1586

column1: What is a principal role of plasma transfusion in neonatal care?
column2:
Plasma. Plasma supplies factors and is used for selected acquired deficiencies, including DIC or liver-related coagulopathy.

PDF p. 1588

column1: Why does a temporal association between red-cell transfusion and NEC not by itself establish causation?
column2:
Severe anemia, evolving illness and reverse causation can confound the association; the chapter reports inconsistent observational and trial evidence.

PDF p. 1578

column1: Which embryologic tissues form the early alimentary canal?
column2:
Endoderm and splanchnic mesoderm. Folding of endoderm and splanchnic mesoderm produces the early gut tube.

PDF p. 1596

column1: Why is esophageal blood supply described as segmental?
column2:
Different esophageal regions receive distinct arterial branches. Segmental arterial inputs matter when preserving perfusion during mobilization.

PDF p. 1596

column1: How does normal intestinal fixation reduce the risk of midgut volvulus?
column2:
It creates a broad mesenteric base that resists twisting. Widely separated fixation points broaden the mesenteric base and reduce twisting risk.

PDF p. 1599

column1: What is the major digestive and absorptive portion of the gastrointestinal tract?
column2:
Small intestine. The small intestine is the major digestive and absorptive region; villi and microvilli greatly increase surface area.

PDF p. 1601

column1: What are the two basic functions of the colon described in the chapter?
column2:
Water-electrolyte absorption and storage/elimination of feces. The colon absorbs water and electrolytes and stores and eliminates feces.

PDF p. 1601

column1: Why can a normally positioned colon fail to exclude abnormal duodenal rotation?
column2:
Duodenal and colonic rotation are not completely codependent; one can be abnormal while the other appears appropriately rotated.

PDF p. 1601

column1: What distinguishes gastroesophageal reflux disease from physiologic reflux?
column2:
GERD requires medical complications attributable to reflux. GER is retrograde flow; GERD denotes a pathologic condition causing complications. Regurgitation alone is insufficient.

PDF p. 1603

column1: What is the major mechanism allowing reflux in term and preterm infants?
column2:
Transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations. Transient relaxations unrelated to swallowing permit retrograde passage; even very small infants can have good basal sphincter tone.

PDF p. 1603

column1: How do pH monitoring and multichannel intraluminal impedance differ?
column2:
Multichannel intraluminal impedance. Impedance detects fluid presence regardless of pH; combined sensors can characterize acid and nonacid events.

PDF p. 1605

column1: Does a reflux event preceding apnea prove that reflux caused apnea?
column2:
Temporal association alone does not prove causality. The chapter explicitly cautions that sequence does not establish a causal link.

PDF p. 1605

column1: What management approach is emphasized for infant GERD in the source?
column2:
Conservative expectant management with clinical reassessment. The source favors conservative management because symptoms often improve and drug or surgical safety and efficacy are limited.

PDF p. 1608

column1: Why may an upper gastrointestinal contrast series fail to establish GERD?
column2:
It captures a brief interval; observing reflux does not establish frequency, complications or causality, though the study can assess relevant anatomy.

PDF p. 1605

column1: What does a low stool osmotic gap suggest?
column2:
Electrolyte transport-related diarrhea. A low gap supports electrolyte transport-related diarrhea; unabsorbed dietary solutes tend to produce a high gap.

PDF p. 1615

column1: Why may fecal elastase be falsely low in watery diarrhea?
column2:
Dilution can lower the measured concentration. Watery diarrhea can dilute fecal elastase; maturation and clinical context also affect interpretation.

PDF p. 1615

column1: What acid-base pattern can occur in congenital chloride diarrhea?
column2:
Hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Loss of chloride and sodium through defective intestinal chloride-bicarbonate exchange can cause volume contraction and metabolic alkalosis.

PDF p. 1617

column1: Why can breast milk and lactose-containing formula both provoke glucose-galactose malabsorption symptoms?
column2:
Defective SGLT1-mediated glucose and galactose absorption. Lactose digestion releases glucose and galactose; failure of their transport leaves osmoles in the lumen.

PDF p. 1618

column1: What pattern suggests an inherited intestinal zinc absorption defect?
column2:
Zinc deficiency from acrodermatitis enteropathica. SLC39A4-related zinc malabsorption causes the characteristic dermatitis and diarrhea; supplementation is required long term.

PDF p. 1618

column1: How is the stool osmotic gap calculated in the chapter?
column2:
Estimated gap = 290 − 2 × (stool sodium + stool potassium), using compatible concentration units; low and high gaps support different mechanisms and are interpreted clinically.

PDF p. 1615

column1: What typical presentation suggests hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
column2:
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Progressive nonbilious projectile emesis in early infancy with contraction alkalosis is the classic pattern.

PDF p. 1636

column1: What developmental mechanism is associated with intrinsic duodenal atresia or stenosis?
column2:
Failure of recanalization after epithelial proliferation. The embryonic duodenum transiently becomes solid; failure of recanalization is linked to intrinsic atresia or stenosis.

PDF p. 1638

column1: Why can malrotation predispose to ischemic bowel injury?
column2:
Twisting of the mesentery compromising bowel blood supply. Improper fixation permits twisting around the mesenteric vascular axis and can compromise perfusion.

PDF p. 1640

column1: What mechanism produces obstruction in Hirschsprung disease?
column2:
Arrested development of the myenteric nervous system. Congenital intestinal aganglionosis produces a functionally obstructed distal segment.

PDF p. 1645

column1: Why does bilious emesis in a neonate require urgent evaluation?
column2:
Malrotation with midgut volvulus. The chapter emphasizes urgent exclusion of malrotation and volvulus because delay can allow ischemic bowel injury.

PDF p. 1650

column1: Which test is emphasized for evaluating suspected hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
column2:
Ultrasonography has high diagnostic utility for the thickened and elongated pyloric channel; interpretation is integrated with the clinical presentation.

PDF p. 1650

column1: What combination should raise concern for NEC in a preterm infant?
column2:
Possible NEC requiring integrated clinical, laboratory and imaging evaluation. The combination is concerning for intestinal disease and systemic deterioration, although individual signs are nonspecific.

PDF p. 1652

column1: What are important limitations of radiographic pneumatosis assessment?
column2:
Stool may mimic pneumatosis and absence of clear pneumatosis does not exclude disease. The source describes both misinterpretation of stool and disease progression without classic gas findings.

PDF p. 1652

column1: What are the principal initial medical measures for suspected NEC?
column2:
Stop enteral feeds, decompress the gut, provide antibiotics and support physiology. Medical management targets bowel rest, decompression, infection coverage and metabolic, hematologic, respiratory and circulatory support.

PDF p. 1653

column1: Which radiographic finding is an absolute surgical-intervention criterion in the source discussion?
column2:
It establishes pneumoperitoneum and an absolute criterion for intervention. The chapter identifies pneumoperitoneum as an absolute intervention criterion, while acknowledging that perforation can have different etiologies.

PDF p. 1654

column1: Why is human milk relevant to NEC prevention?
column2:
It is associated with less NEC and provides immune and barrier-supporting components. Human milk is associated with reduced NEC and has multiple protective bioactive constituents; risk is not eliminated.

PDF p. 1657

column1: Why should age at onset alone not be used to distinguish NEC from spontaneous intestinal perforation?
column2:
SIP often presents earlier, but substantial timing overlap occurs, especially within the first two weeks; anatomy, imaging, operative and pathologic findings may be needed.

PDF p. 1661

column1: Why can glucose measurements differ between plasma and whole blood?
column2:
Plasma and whole-blood values differ and delayed handling permits glycolysis. Whole-blood and plasma values differ; ongoing cellular glycolysis can lower an inadequately handled sample result.

PDF p. 1671

column1: Which infants are among the groups monitored for hypoglycemia in the source?
column2:
An infant of a diabetic mother. Infants of diabetic mothers, growth abnormalities, prematurity and acute illness are among monitored risk groups.

PDF p. 1685

column1: Why is persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia particularly hazardous?
column2:
Insulin restricts endogenous glucose release and alternative fuel availability. Excess insulin inhibits glycogenolysis and availability of alternate fuels, increasing the risk of brain injury.

PDF p. 1680

column1: Why can a preterm infant develop hyperglycemia despite a reasonable exogenous glucose infusion?
column2:
Persistent endogenous glucose production with immature insulin regulation. Prematurity, stress, endogenous production and altered insulin effects contribute; medications and sepsis may also be relevant.

PDF p. 1689

column1: How can activating KATP-channel mutations cause neonatal diabetes?
column2:
Failure of channel closure impairs insulin secretion. Activating channel mutations prevent normal closure and inhibit beta-cell insulin release.

PDF p. 1690

column1: What three tasks frame management of neonatal hypoglycemia?
column2:
Anticipate infants at risk, promptly correct low glucose and investigate and treat the underlying cause, especially when episodes persist or recur.

PDF p. 1685

column1: Which fraction of circulating calcium is physiologically active?
column2:
Ionized calcium. Ionized calcium is the active fraction; total calcium also includes protein-bound and complexed fractions.

PDF p. 1693

column1: How can a high phosphate load contribute to late neonatal hypocalcemia?
column2:
Limited renal phosphorus excretion and immature response to PTH. Immature renal handling and relative PTH resistance can promote phosphate retention and lower calcium.

PDF p. 1709

column1: Why should magnesium be considered in an infant with hypocalcemia?
column2:
Hypomagnesemia can coexist with impaired parathyroid function and hypocalcemia. Magnesium deficiency may impair PTH-related calcium regulation; the source describes improvement in calcium and PTH with correction in relevant infants.

PDF p. 1716

column1: Which maternal treatment can produce neonatal hypermagnesemia?
column2:
Magnesium sulfate. Maternal magnesium sulfate can raise fetal and neonatal magnesium; renal function affects clearance.

PDF p. 1718

column1: How does early birth increase the risk of metabolic bone disease?
column2:
Loss of late-gestation calcium and phosphorus accretion. Premature delivery interrupts fetal mineral accretion; postnatal nutrition and illness add to risk.

PDF p. 1719

column1: Why may tremors or seizures fail to distinguish hypocalcemia from hypomagnesemia?
column2:
Their neuromuscular manifestations overlap, and the deficiencies can coexist; laboratory assessment is needed rather than symptom labeling alone.

PDF p. 1716

column1: Why is newborn screening important for congenital hypothyroidism?
column2:
Early detection and treatment can prevent neurodevelopmental disability. The chapter emphasizes prevention of neurodevelopmental consequences through early recognition and treatment.

PDF p. 1735

column1: Why can TSH-only screening miss central hypothyroidism?
column2:
Pituitary or hypothalamic deficiency may not produce high TSH. Central hypothyroidism can have normal or only mildly elevated TSH; T4-based assessment is needed when suspected.

PDF p. 1734

column1: What is the source principle on timing replacement for confirmed or strongly suspected congenital hypothyroidism?
column2:
Start replacement promptly rather than delaying for a complete etiologic workup. Treatment should begin promptly after confirmatory sampling; maternal T4 protection is temporary and delays can harm development.

PDF p. 1739

column1: Can neonatal Graves disease occur after maternal thyroidectomy or radioiodine treatment?
column2:
Persistent maternal stimulating TSH-receptor antibodies crossing the placenta. Maternal receptor-stimulating antibodies may persist after treatment and cross the placenta.

PDF p. 1741

column1: How can a thyroxine-binding globulin defect affect thyroid tests?
column2:
An inherited thyroid-hormone binding protein abnormality. TBG excess or deficiency can change total hormone concentrations while free T4 remains normal.

PDF p. 1743

column1: Why must neonatal TSH and free T4 be interpreted using age-appropriate values?
column2:
The neonatal thyroid axis changes after birth; developmental reference intervals and the clinical context prevent inappropriate interpretation using adult values.

PDF p. 1728

column1: Which fetal signal induces müllerian duct regression?
column2:
Müllerian duct structures. AMH acts locally to induce müllerian regression; testosterone instead supports wolffian differentiation.

PDF p. 1752

column1: How is dihydrotestosterone produced for external genital differentiation?
column2:
5-alpha-reductase conversion to dihydrotestosterone. 5-alpha-reductase generates DHT from testosterone in peripheral tissues; DHT is the potent androgen emphasized for external differentiation.

PDF p. 1754

column1: What elements form the initial evaluation of a newborn with suspected DSD?
column2:
Chromosome assessment, pelvic/renal imaging and relevant adrenal hormones/electrolytes. First-tier evaluation integrates chromosomes, anatomy and biochemistry; gonadal findings help direct hormone studies.

PDF p. 1760

column1: Why must 17-hydroxyprogesterone and testosterone be interpreted by age and illness status?
column2:
Prematurity, illness and neonatal hormone changes can affect the result. The source notes elevated 17-OHP in premature or sick infants and physiologic testosterone surges; results need contextual confirmation.

PDF p. 1761

column1: What should early discussion with the family include?
column2:
A private, calm discussion explaining findings, consultations, uncertainty and expected timing. Experienced clinicians should provide privacy, explain the evaluation and support bonding while information develops.

PDF p. 1759

column1: Which fetal hormone supports development of wolffian ducts?
column2:
Locally produced testosterone supports ipsilateral wolffian duct differentiation; this role differs from AMH-driven müllerian regression and DHT-dependent external differentiation.

PDF p. 1752

column1: Does the absence of a family history exclude an inborn error of metabolism?
column2:
An inherited metabolic disorder remains possible. Most affected neonates may lack similarly affected relatives; recessive inheritance and new variants help explain this.

PDF p. 1786

column1: Can documented infection exclude an underlying metabolic disorder?
column2:
Continue it because infection and metabolic disease can coexist. The chapter specifically notes that metabolic disorders can predispose to sepsis, including galactosemia with E. coli infection.

PDF p. 1787

column1: Which initial blood tests help classify a suspected neonatal metabolic disorder?
column2:
Glucose, blood gas, electrolytes, lactate, ketones and ammonia. The source core screening set uses these tests to identify glucose, acid-base, energy and nitrogen-disposal disturbances.

PDF p. 1832

column1: What is the most effective general approach to metabolic acidosis?
column2:
Identify and treat the cause while supporting physiology. The source emphasizes cause-directed treatment and assessment of common systemic causes as well as inborn errors.

PDF p. 1840

column1: What clinical pattern should prompt immediate evaluation for hyperammonemia?
column2:
Plasma ammonia with appropriate specimen handling. Hyperammonemia may progress rapidly to coma and irreversible neurologic injury; immediate investigation is essential.

PDF p. 1856

column1: Why must collection and handling instructions be established before specialized metabolic samples are obtained?
column2:
Preanalytic requirements affect whether results are interpretable; rapid screening and specialist tests require reliable sampling rather than indiscriminate collection.

PDF p. 1831

column1: Why is albumin binding important in unconjugated bilirubin physiology?
column2:
Albumin binding influences the unbound fraction available to enter tissues. Unconjugated bilirubin is poorly water soluble and circulates bound to albumin; binding capacity influences biologic availability.

PDF p. 1871

column1: Which signs are concerning for acute bilirubin encephalopathy?
column2:
Acute bilirubin encephalopathy. This constellation is described in acute bilirubin encephalopathy and calls for urgent management of severe hyperbilirubinemia.

PDF p. 1896

column1: What chemical changes underlie bilirubin phototherapy?
column2:
Photoisomerization including formation of more readily eliminated bilirubin isomers. Light changes bilirubin configuration and structure, including formation of lumirubin, facilitating elimination.

PDF p. 1908

column1: Which patient variables are necessary for the chapter’s 2022 phototherapy threshold graphs?
column2:
Postnatal age in hours, gestational age and relevant neurotoxicity risk factors. The reproduced graphs separate gestation, age in hours and risk-factor groups; an isolated bilirubin number is insufficient.

PDF p. 1923

column1: Is conjugated hyperbilirubinemia physiologic neonatal jaundice?
column2:
A pathologic bile secretion or flow problem requiring evaluation. The chapter calls conjugated hyperbilirubinemia always pathologic; its differential includes obstructive, hepatocellular, infectious and metabolic disease.

PDF p. 1922

column1: Why can normal stool pigmentation very early in jaundice fail to exclude biliary atresia?
column2:
Acholic stools may appear only later; clinical obstruction and even biopsy features can be nonspecific early, so evolving cholestasis needs timely evaluation.

PDF p. 1928

column1: What does serum sodium concentration represent compared with total-body sodium?
column2:
Concentration reflects sodium relative to water, while total sodium content influences extracellular volume. The concentration is a salt-water relationship; total sodium content is a major determinant of extracellular volume.

PDF p. 1942

column1: Why can very preterm infants have high insensible water losses?
column2:
Greater transepidermal evaporative loss through immature skin. Immature skin contributes substantially to evaporative loss; environment and treatments also influence requirements.

PDF p. 1944

column1: What broad mechanisms can produce neonatal hyponatremia?
column2:
Water retention, excessive sodium loss or inadequate sodium intake. The chapter classifies hyponatremia through water handling, sodium losses and intake; clinical volume assessment separates them.

PDF p. 1947

column1: What three questions organize acid-base interpretation?
column2:
Identify the primary abnormality, secondary compensation and whether compensation is appropriate. pH, bicarbonate and carbon dioxide together establish the primary process and adequacy of compensation; mixed disorders occur.

PDF p. 1953

column1: Why can chloride and volume depletion maintain metabolic alkalosis?
column2:
Volume and chloride depletion favor bicarbonate retention and impaired alkali excretion. Reduced filtration and enhanced sodium-bicarbonate reabsorption, together with hormonal effects, help maintain alkalosis.

PDF p. 1954

column1: Why are premature infants less able to compensate for an acute acid load?
column2:
Tubular immaturity limits bicarbonate conservation, urinary acidification and ammonium generation; low filtration also limits available urinary buffers.

PDF p. 1953

column1: What does serum creatinine immediately after birth substantially reflect?
column2:
The initial value reflects maternal creatinine as well as neonatal transition. Immediately after birth, creatinine reflects the maternal concentration; the postnatal trend and gestation are important.

PDF p. 1965

column1: Why is bag-collected urine unsuitable for confirming a neonatal UTI?
column2:
Fecal contamination can cause false positives; obtain an appropriate culture specimen. A bag can provide urinalysis material but is not recommended for culture confirmation; catheterization is more reliable.

PDF p. 1965

column1: What does glycosuria with phosphate and amino-acid wasting suggest?
column2:
Generalized proximal tubular dysfunction. Combined urinary solute losses suggest a proximal tubulopathy such as Fanconi syndrome.

PDF p. 1967

column1: Why can prolonged renal hypoperfusion progress beyond a functional prerenal problem?
column2:
Acute tubular injury after a prolonged prerenal state. Prolonged hypoperfusion can lead to intrinsic tubular injury; perinatal illness and nephrotoxins are relevant risks.

PDF p. 1968

column1: Which study is diagnostic for posterior urethral valves?
column2:
Voiding cystourethrogram. VCUG demonstrates the posterior urethral obstruction and associated reflux; treatment centers on securing urinary drainage.

PDF p. 1978

column1: Which embryonic renal structure becomes the definitive kidney?
column2:
The metanephros forms the definitive kidney through reciprocal development of ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme.

PDF p. 1960

column1: Which physiologic roles make skin integrity especially important in newborns?
column2:
Barrier to water loss and infection control. Skin supports water balance, thermoregulation and host defense; injury can therefore have systemic consequences.

PDF p. 1985

column1: What typical features support erythema toxicum?
column2:
Erythema toxicum. The source describes an evanescent, sterile, eosinophil-rich benign eruption, usually arising after birth.

PDF p. 1990

column1: What sequence characterizes transient neonatal pustular melanosis?
column2:
Transient neonatal pustular melanosis. The eruption progresses from superficial pustules to collarettes and residual pigmented macules, and stages may coexist at birth.

PDF p. 1990

column1: What is emphasized for postnatal diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa?
column2:
Next-generation sequencing, with selected biopsy-based studies for special situations. The source describes genetic diagnosis, with immunofluorescence mapping or electron microscopy reserved for selected situations.

PDF p. 1997

column1: What mechanism links neonatal lupus skin disease and congenital heart block?
column2:
Transplacental maternal autoantibodies. Maternal anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB antibodies can produce transient cutaneous disease and congenital heart block; mothers may be asymptomatic.

PDF p. 2014

column1: How does palm and sole involvement differ between two common benign pustular eruptions?
column2:
Erythema toxicum rarely affects palms or soles, whereas transient neonatal pustular melanosis can occur there; morphology, timing and the infant’s condition still guide the assessment.

PDF p. 1990

column1: What should an abnormal neonatal red reflex prompt?
column2:
An important abnormal observation requiring immediate ophthalmologic evaluation. Leukocoria is a descriptive finding with serious differential diagnoses; prompt assessment is required.

PDF p. 2035

column1: Which symptom triad suggests congenital glaucoma?
column2:
Congenital glaucoma. Raised intraocular pressure can stretch the eye and damage vision; tearing, photophobia and blepharospasm are classic symptoms.

PDF p. 2034

column1: What serious diagnosis must be considered when assessing infant tearing?
column2:
Congenital glaucoma. Nasolacrimal obstruction is common, but glaucoma is a particularly important alternative in the tearing infant.

PDF p. 2031

column1: What anatomic abnormality defines cataract?
column2:
Cataract. Cataract denotes lens opacity; neonatal causes include hereditary, metabolic, infectious, traumatic and other conditions.

PDF p. 2036

column1: Which neonatal or infant malignancy commonly presents with leukocoria or strabismus?
column2:
Retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is the most frequent malignant intraocular tumor in children and may present with leukocoria or strabismus.

PDF p. 2043

column1: Why should a lens opacity in a newborn prompt consideration of systemic disease?
column2:
Cataracts may accompany metabolic, infectious, hereditary and syndromic conditions; defining the opacity alone does not establish its cause.

PDF p. 2036

column1: What distinguishes the two simplified phases of ROP?
column2:
Early relative hyperoxia suppresses VEGF; later avascular retinal hypoxia raises VEGF. Early growth suppression leaves avascular retina; later hypoxia stimulates excessive VEGF and abnormal vessels.

PDF p. 2055

column1: Why is simply minimizing oxygen not a complete prevention strategy?
column2:
Retinal risk must be balanced with survival and other morbidity. The chapter discusses lower ROP treatment rates alongside higher death and NEC, illustrating competing risks.

PDF p. 2056

column1: What does stage 3 ROP describe, and what does plus disease add?
column2:
Stage 3 with plus disease. Stage 3 is extraretinal neovascularization; plus disease describes pronounced venous dilation and arterial tortuosity.

PDF p. 2057

column1: Why are serial retinal examinations necessary in at-risk premature infants?
column2:
Continue scheduled retinal surveillance according to regional criteria and findings. ROP evolves with retinal maturation; repeated examinations detect progression while treatment can preserve vision.

PDF p. 2057

column1: Why is peripheral avascular retina ablated in selected sight-threatening ROP?
column2:
Avascular peripheral retina overproducing angiogenic signals. Laser reduces the angiogenic drive from avascular retina to prevent progression and detachment, at the cost of peripheral retinal tissue.

PDF p. 2059

column1: Why does anti-VEGF treatment require careful longer-term surveillance and risk discussion?
column2:
Recurrence can occur later than after laser, and systemic VEGF suppression raises unresolved developmental concerns; treatment selection and follow-up require specialist judgment.

PDF p. 2060

column1: How does developmental timing distinguish malformations from deformations in the source?
column2:
Deformation of an essentially formed part. Early embryonic disturbances produce malformations; later fetal influences can alter the configuration of essentially normal structures.

PDF p. 2065

column1: Which circumstances can increase fetal constraint and positional deformity?
column2:
Increased uterine compression affecting fetal position and motion. Oligohydramnios and other constraint factors may produce contractures and angular or torsional changes; some resolve, others require care.

PDF p. 2067

column1: What posture is characteristic of upper brachial plexus injury?
column2:
Upper brachial plexus palsy. The described waiter’s-tip posture is characteristic of the common upper plexus injury pattern.

PDF p. 2068

column1: Why should clavicular fracture be considered in a newborn with reduced arm movement?
column2:
Pain-related pseudoparalysis from fracture. Clavicular fracture can cause painful reduced motion and mimic a neurologic palsy; examination and imaging distinguish causes.

PDF p. 2069

column1: Why can routine radiographs miss proximal humeral epiphyseal separation at birth?
column2:
The proximal humeral epiphysis is not yet ossified. An unossified epiphysis can conceal separation on plain radiography; ultrasound or other imaging and later callus may help.

PDF p. 2070

column1: Why must infection remain in the differential of a newborn with decreased active limb movement?
column2:
Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis can also cause painful reduced movement, so delivery trauma or nerve injury should not be assumed from pseudoparalysis alone.

PDF p. 2069

column1: Can a neonate with bone or joint infection lack prominent fever or leukocytosis?
column2:
Skeletal infection remains possible despite subtle systemic findings. Immature neonatal responses may produce subtle signs; reduced movement, feeding intolerance or irritability can be early clues.

PDF p. 2072
